overview.title: Learn
overview.intro: Choose a technique to see a worked example or try it on a practice grid.
difficultyParagraphs: A puzzle’s level comes from the hardest technique in its rated solution. Repeating an easier move does not raise the level. New games start at Medium by default.
Beginner and Easy cover singles. Medium introduces candidate removals. Tricky follows a digit across houses, and Hard adds wings and uniqueness techniques.
Very Hard introduces chains and coloring. Expert and Master use longer chains, groups of candidates, and almost locked sets. Extreme adds forcing proofs and patterns that span the grid.
Impossible is the highest level. Some puzzles at this level need many separate cases or a computer search.
Within each level, the foundation lessons come before the techniques that use them. Classic Sudoku comes first. The later sections cover extra rules such as cage totals and marked diagonals.

fundamentals.title: Fundamentals
fundamentals.summary: Every row, column, and box needs each digit from 1 through 9 exactly once. The digits already in those three places tell you which numbers can still go in an empty cell.

blocks.title: Check a cell’s row, column, and box

paragraphs: Choose an empty cell. Look along its row, down its column, and inside its box. Each digit you see there rules out that digit in your cell.

blocks.title: Houses

paragraphs: A classic Sudoku has nine rows, nine columns, and nine boxes. Each must contain the digits 1 through 9 exactly once. The thick borders mark the 3×3 boxes.
A row, a column, or a box is called a house. A row or column is also called a line. The digits printed at the start are the givens.

blocks.title: Cell addresses

paragraphs: R2C4 means row 2, column 4. Count down two rows from the top and across four columns from the left.
Number the boxes from left to right, one band at a time. Box 1 is at the top left. Box 9 is at the bottom right.

blocks.title: Cells that see each other

paragraphs: Two different cells see each other if they share a row, column, or box. These cells are peers. Only one of them can contain a particular digit.
For example, R2C4 sees R2C5 along row 2. It sees R3C4 down column 4 and R3C5 inside box 2.

blocks.title: Candidates

paragraphs: A candidate is a digit that can still go in an empty cell. The small pencil marks record these choices.

blocks.title: Read a diagram

paragraphs: Blue marks a candidate to examine. Red marks a candidate to remove. Green marks a digit you can place.

copy.description: Row 2 already contains 2, 4, and 9. Remove those choices from R2C4.
copy.reason: Column 4 rules out 1, 5, 6, 7, and 8. Box 2 adds no other digits to that list. R2C4 can only be 3.

paragraphs: If a cell has one candidate left, place it. This move is called a naked single.

blocks.title: Place a single
blocks.instruction: Find a cell with one candidate. Place that digit.

groups.title: Beginner
groups.overview: Fill the last gap in a house or the only place for a digit in a box.

lessons.title: Which cells see each other?
lessons.summary: Two cells see each other when they share a row, column, or box. A 5 in either cell rules out 5 in the other. This is what Sudoku players mean when they say that two cells are peers.

blocks.title: Trace a digit’s row, column, and box

paragraphs: Choose a 5 on the grid. Follow its row, its column, and the edges of its box.

blocks.title: One shared house is enough

paragraphs: Every other cell in those three houses sees the 5. Sudoku players call these cells its peers. None can contain another 5.

blocks.title: What a pencil mark tells you

paragraphs: The same rule applies to pencil marks. If two cells in one row both show a possible 5, only one can be 5.
If you remove one of the marks, the other is still only a possibility. The row can have another place for 5.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: R2C2 and R3C3 share neither a row nor a column. Do they see each other?
questions.explanation: Both cells are in box 1. Sharing that box is enough.

questions.prompt: If R2C2 is 5, does that rule out 5 in R4C4?
questions.explanation: R4C4 is outside row 2, column 2, and box 1.

lessons.title: Full House
lessons.summary: A row with eight filled cells already tells you its ninth digit. The same rule works in a column or box. This last placement is called a Full House.

blocks.title: Look for one empty cell

paragraphs: Scan for a row, column, or box with eight filled cells. Count from 1 to 9 and mark which digit is missing.
For example, if a box contains 1, 2, 3, 4, 6, 7, 8, and 9, its last cell must be 5.

lessons.title: Hidden Single in a Box
lessons.summary: A box needs one copy of each digit. Sometimes the rows and columns around it leave just one cell for a missing digit, even though the cell still has several pencil marks.

blocks.title: Scan the rows and columns that cross the box

items: Pick a digit that appears several times on the grid.
Find a box that still needs it.
Follow each placed copy along its row or column into the box. Rule out the cells on those lines.
If only one empty cell remains possible in the box, place the digit there.

paragraphs: A cell can have several pencil marks and still be the only place in the box for one of them.

groups.title: Easy
groups.overview: Look for a cell with one choice or a digit with one place in a house.

lessons.title: Hidden Single
lessons.summary: A hidden single is the only place a digit can go in a row, column, or box. The cell can still have several candidates. The digit has only one home in that house.

blocks.title: Count the places for one digit

paragraphs: Pick a row, column, or box that still needs a digit. Find every empty cell in that house where the digit can go.
If only one cell remains, place the digit there. You can erase the other pencil marks in that cell.

blocks.title: Where to look for blockers

items: For a row, check its empty cells against their columns and boxes.
For a column, check its empty cells against their rows and boxes.
For a box, look along the rows and columns that cross it. A placed copy rules out that digit along its line.

lessons.title: Naked Single
lessons.summary: A naked single is a cell with only one possible digit. Once its row, column, and box rule out the other eight, you can fill the cell.

blocks.title: Count the candidates in one cell

paragraphs: Choose an empty cell near several different placed digits. Look for those digits in its row, column, and box.
If these houses rule out eight different digits, the ninth goes in the cell. For example, if only 4 remains, place 4.
A removal can also reveal a single. After you remove 6 from a cell marked {2, 6}, place 2.

groups.title: Medium
groups.overview: Use a line, a box, or a small group of cells to remove candidates.

lessons.title: Candidates and eliminations
lessons.summary: A pencil mark records a digit that can still go in a cell. A deduction can rule out that digit before you know which one belongs there.

blocks.title: Check which pencil marks are possible

paragraphs: Before you count candidates, make sure your notes include every digit still possible in the cells you use. An empty pencil-mark slot can also mean you never marked it.

blocks.title: Possible does not mean certain

paragraphs: A candidate is a possibility. A removal means you can explain why that digit cannot go in that cell.
After a removal, look for a cell with one candidate or a house with one place for a digit.

blocks.caption: Three things you can say about 8 in R3C6

blocks.title: Count cells and distinct digits

paragraphs: Suppose two cells in row 3 each show only 2 and 8. The cells must be different, so together they use both digits. Remove 2 and 8 from the other cells in row 3.
Count each different digit once. Two pencil marks for 2 still represent one digit.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: You marked 2 and 8 in a cell but never checked 5. Can you rely on that cell having just two choices?
questions.explanation: First find out whether 5 can go there. The missing pencil mark alone cannot rule it out.

questions.prompt: Can a candidate removal help even if it leaves no single?
questions.explanation: The removal can leave a pair, a link, or another pattern you can use next.

questions.prompt: Two cells each show {2, 8}. How many different digits are in their lists?
questions.explanation: Only 2 and 8 appear. Each counts once.

lessons.title: Locked Candidates
lessons.summary: Sometimes every place for a box’s missing digit lies on one row. The box must supply that row’s copy, so the digit can go nowhere else in the row. The same reasoning works with columns.

blocks.title: Find where a line crosses a box

paragraphs: Highlight one digit. Look for a box where all its possible places lie in one row or column. You can also start with a line whose places all lie in one box.
One cell in the overlap must contain the digit. That single placement supplies the digit to both houses.

blocks.title: Pointing from a box

paragraphs: For pointing, start inside the box. If all its 6s lie in row 4, remove 6 from row 4 outside the box. Two such places form a pointing pair. Three form a pointing triple.

blocks.title: Claiming from a line

paragraphs: For claiming, start along the line. If every possible 6 in row 4 lies in box 5, remove 6 from the other rows of box 5.

references.label: Diagonal Locked Candidates in X Sudoku

lessons.title: Counting cells and digits
lessons.summary: Three cells in one row need three different digits. If only three digits fit among them, the rest of the row cannot use those digits. This counting rule also works in a column or box.

blocks.title: Compare the number of cells and digits

paragraphs: Pick a row, column, or box with a few short candidate lists. Start with two or three cells.

blocks.title: Start with the cells

paragraphs: Suppose three cells in one row allow only 2, 5, and 8 between them. Each cell needs a different digit. Those three cells use all three digits, in some order.

blocks.title: Start with the missing digits

paragraphs: You can also start with digits. Suppose only R6C2 and R6C6 can contain 3 or 8 in row 6. Those cells must hold 3 and 8. Remove their other candidates.

blocks.caption: What an equal count tells you
rows: As many distinct digits as cells
Those digits in other cells of the house
Selected missing digits in a house
As many possible cells as digits

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Three cells show {2, 4}, {4, 7}, and {2, 7}. How many different digits appear?
questions.explanation: There are three digits, 2, 4, and 7.

questions.prompt: Only two cells in a box allow 2 or 9. Where can you remove other digits?
options: From the rest of the box
questions.explanation: The box needs both 2 and 9. Those two cells must hold them.

questions.prompt: Three cells in one row have four candidate digits between them. Does that reserve all four?
questions.explanation: The three cells use three different digits. The fourth digit can go elsewhere.

lessons.title: Naked Subsets
lessons.summary: A naked subset is a group of cells in one house with exactly as many different candidates as cells. Those cells use all those digits, in some order. The rest of the house cannot use them.

blocks.title: Compare short candidate lists

paragraphs: Start with a row, column, or box. Look for two cells with the same two candidates. For a larger subset, add cells and count all the different digits.
If three cells have only three digits between them, those cells must use all three. The same count works for two or four cells.

blocks.title: Naked pair

paragraphs: Suppose two cells in one row each allow only 4 and 6. One must be 4 and the other 6. Remove both digits from the rest of the row.

blocks.title: Naked triple

paragraphs: Look for lists such as {2, 3}, {2, 5}, and {3, 5} in one house. Together they use 2, 3, and 5. Remove all three digits from its other cells.

blocks.title: Naked quadruple

paragraphs: Four cells with {1, 2}, {2, 4}, {3, 4}, and {1, 2, 3} use exactly four different digits. If they share a house, remove 1, 2, 3, and 4 elsewhere in it.

blocks.title: Locked pair

paragraphs: If both cells of a pair share a line and a box, each house gets both digits. Remove them from the other cells in both houses.

blocks.title: Locked triple

paragraphs: Three cells can fill the whole overlap between a line and a box. A triple there also removes its digits from both houses. Only three cells fit in the overlap.

lessons.title: Hidden Subsets
lessons.summary: A hidden subset forms when a group of digits has just enough cells to hold it in one house. Those cells belong to the group, so you can erase their other candidates.

blocks.title: Count the places for a few digits

paragraphs: Pick a missing digit with few possible places in a house. Look for another digit that can go only in those same cells.
Count all the places for the chosen digits in that house. If three digits have only three cells, the three cells must hold those digits.

blocks.title: Hidden pair

paragraphs: If 2 and 7 appear only in the same two cells of a row, those cells must hold 2 and 7. Remove their other candidates.

blocks.title: Hidden triple

paragraphs: For three digits, count every cell that shows at least one of them. If there are just three such cells, remove their other marks.

blocks.title: Hidden quadruple

paragraphs: For four digits, look for exactly four cells that contain any of them. Look through the whole house before you remove other marks from those cells.

groups.title: Tricky
groups.overview: Trace one digit through two or more houses.

lessons.title: Strong and weak links
lessons.summary: A link says what one candidate tells you about another. A strong link needs at least one end to be true. A weak link allows at most one true end. A pair can have both properties.

blocks.title: Compare two places with three

paragraphs: Highlight 5. Find a row with just two possible 5s, then a row with three. Compare what happens in each row if you remove one possible 5.
Each end of a link stands for a claim, such as “R4C2 is 5.” A solid line shows a strong link. A dashed line shows a weak link. An arrow shows which end you use first.

blocks.title: A weak link comes from a conflict

paragraphs: A weak link means at most one end is true. If R4C2 is 5, R4C5 cannot be 5 because both cells share row 4.
Two digits in one cell also conflict. If that cell is 2, it cannot also be 7. Both choices can be false if the cell has a third candidate.

blocks.title: A strong link comes from a required choice

paragraphs: A strong link means at least one end is true. Suppose row 4 has just two places for 5, R4C2 and R4C8. If you rule out 5 in R4C2, row 4 forces 5 into R4C8.
Look through the entire row. A third possible 5 breaks this argument.

blocks.title: One pair can have both links

paragraphs: A pair that has both properties is a dual link. Exactly one end is true. The only two places for 5 in a row form a dual link, as do the only two candidates in a cell.

blocks.caption: Which pairs of states can each link allow?

blocks.title: What each link guarantees

paragraphs: A strong link alone allows both ends to be true. To use the same pair as a weak link, you also need a reason the ends cannot both be true.

blocks.title: Where to use links

paragraphs: In a Skyscraper, two rows each have only two places for a digit. Two of those places share a column. The row pairs supply strong links, and the column supplies a weak link.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: A row has three possible 7s. After you remove one, must a particular cell be 7?
questions.explanation: Either of the two remaining cells can supply the 7.

questions.prompt: A cell allows only 3 and 9. Which links do those two choices have?
questions.explanation: The cell needs one digit and has room for only one. Exactly one of the candidates is true.

questions.prompt: Two candidates have a strong link. Without a separate conflict, can both be true?
questions.explanation: A strong link requires at least one true end. Both can be true.
