lessons.title: Counting rows and columns
lessons.summary: Two rows can reserve two columns for a digit before you know its exact cells. Each row needs a copy, and the copies need different columns. That leaves no room for another copy in either column.

blocks.title: Count the rows and columns for one digit

paragraphs: Highlight one digit. Choose rows with only a few places for it. Find every column those rows can use for that digit.

blocks.title: The rows need a place each

paragraphs: The chosen rows are called bases. The columns that cover all their candidates are called covers. Each row needs one copy of the digit. Each column has room for just one.
If two rows can use only two columns, each row must use a different one. Three rows and three columns work the same way.

blocks.title: Where the count removes a candidate

paragraphs: Remove the digit from the cover columns outside the chosen rows. You can turn the pattern sideways by starting with columns.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Every possible 5 in three rows lies in the same three columns. Must those rows use all three columns?
questions.explanation: Each row needs its own 5, and a column has room for only one.

questions.prompt: One of those rows also has a possible 5 in a fourth column. Does the same count still force the first three columns?
questions.explanation: That row can use the fourth column. You need another reason to rule out the extra place.

lessons.title: X-Wing
lessons.summary: In an X-Wing, two rows must put a digit in opposite corners of a rectangle. Either diagonal supplies both columns. That rules out the digit elsewhere in those columns.

blocks.title: Find two rows with matching positions

paragraphs: Choose a digit with two possible places in a row. Look for a second row with that digit in exactly the same two columns.
Each row needs one copy. If the first row uses one column, the second row must use the other. That accounts for the digit in both columns.

blocks.title: Rows and columns

paragraphs: Remove the digit from those columns outside the two rows. If you start with two columns, remove it from the crossing rows instead.

blocks.title: Finned X-Wing

paragraphs: A fin is an extra candidate outside the two cover lines. All fins must share a box. Look in that box for a candidate on a cover line outside the base lines.
If a fin is true, the box rules out the candidate. If all fins are false, the X-Wing rules it out.

blocks.title: Sashimi X-Wing

paragraphs: In a sashimi X-Wing, one base line has only one corner left after you set the fins aside. That corner fixes one placement. The second line needs the other cover. Use the same two cases as for a finned X-Wing.

lessons.title: Skyscraper
lessons.summary: A Skyscraper connects two pairs of places for the same digit. Their aligned ends share a house, so at least one of the two far ends must hold the digit. A cell that sees both far ends cannot hold it.

blocks.title: Look for two pairs with aligned ends

paragraphs: Find a digit with exactly two places in each of two rows. Look for one place in each row in the same column.
The two cells in that column are the aligned ends. The other two cells are the far ends. They must lie in different columns.
If the first far end is false, its row forces the digit into its aligned end. The shared column rules out the other aligned end, so the second row forces its far end.
At least one far end must contain the digit. Remove it from any other cell that sees both. You can also start with two columns.

lessons.title: Two-String Kite
lessons.summary: A Two-String Kite links two possible places in a row to two in a column. A shared box prevents both near ends from holding the digit. One of the far ends must hold it.

blocks.title: Connect a row and a column through a box

paragraphs: Find a row and a column with exactly two places each for the same digit. Use four different cells.
One end from each pair must share a box. The box prevents both of those ends from holding the digit. At least one of the two far ends must hold it. Remove the digit from cells that see both far ends.

blocks.title: Dual kite

paragraphs: Two kites can share the connection in the box. Follow each kite from its own row pair to its own column pair before you remove a candidate.

lessons.title: Empty Rectangle
lessons.summary: In an Empty Rectangle, all the places for one digit in a box lie along two arms of a cross. A pair outside the box can force one arm to supply the digit and rule it out in another cell.

blocks.title: Find the two arms inside a box

paragraphs: Choose a digit in a box. Look for a row and a column that cover all its candidates in the box. Both arms must have a candidate away from their crossing.
The four box cells outside those arms form the empty rectangle. The digit can still be a candidate where the arms cross.
Outside the box, find a line with only two places for the digit. One end must see a whole arm. If that end is true, the box needs the other arm.
Look for a candidate that sees the far end and every place on the other arm. Either choice in the line rules it out.

blocks.title: Removals in the other direction

paragraphs: You can start from either arm. If the target and far end form another two-place line, trace it back for a second removal. A box with just two possible places can also form a short X-Chain.

lessons.title: Swordfish
lessons.summary: A Swordfish reserves three columns for one digit. Three rows need a copy each, and together their candidates fit in just those columns. The other rows must place the digit elsewhere.

blocks.title: Look for three rows that use three columns

paragraphs: Highlight one digit. Choose three rows with two or three possible places each. Count the columns they use between them.
If the candidates fit in just three columns, each row must use a different one. Remove the digit from those columns outside the three rows. You can also start with columns.

blocks.title: Finned Swordfish

paragraphs: For a finned Swordfish, the extra candidates outside the cover lines must share one box. A candidate in that box on a cover line outside the base lines sees every fin.
If a fin is true, the box rules out that candidate. If all fins are false, the three rows need all three covers.

blocks.title: Sashimi Swordfish

paragraphs: In a sashimi Swordfish, at least one base line has a single place left without the fins. That place fixes one cover. The remaining lines still need different covers. Use the same target area as for a finned Swordfish.

groups.title: Hard
groups.overview: Find wings, larger fish, and patterns that depend on a unique solution.

lessons.title: Bivalue cells and cases
lessons.summary: A bivalue cell has exactly two possible digits. One of them must be right. If both choices rule out the same candidate elsewhere, you can remove it without deciding which digit fills the cell.

blocks.title: Compare the two choices in one cell

paragraphs: Find a cell with just two candidates. This is a bivalue cell. Look for other two-candidate cells that see it and share one of its digits.

blocks.title: Cover every choice

paragraphs: Suppose the starting cell, or pivot, has {2, 6}. Cell A sees it and has {2, 9}. Cell B also sees it and has {6, 9}.
If the pivot is 2, A must be 9. If the pivot is 6, B must be 9.
One of the two cells must contain 9. You can remove 9 from another cell that sees both. Leave the pivot open as you compare its two choices.

blocks.title: Check the target in every case

paragraphs: A cell that sees only A can still be 9 in the case that forces B. If the pivot also allows 9, include that third case before you remove anything.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: The pivot allows only 2 and 6. Each choice rules out 9 in R4C4. Can you remove that 9?
questions.explanation: Both possible pivot values rule out the same candidate.

questions.prompt: The pivot also allows 9. You tested only 2 and 6. Have you covered every case?
questions.explanation: You still need to test 9 in the pivot.

questions.prompt: One case forces A to be 9. The other forces B to be 9. Does a cell that sees only A lose 9?
questions.explanation: When B is 9, that cell can still contain 9. A removal must hold in both cases.

lessons.title: XY-Wing
lessons.summary: An XY-Wing links three cells that each have two candidates. Either choice in the middle cell forces the same digit into one of the outside cells. A cell that sees both outside cells cannot hold that digit.

blocks.title: Find a pivot and two wings

paragraphs: Find a cell with two candidates, such as {2, 6}. This is the pivot. Look for two cells that see it, one with {2, 9} and one with {6, 9}.
The two outside cells are the wings. If the pivot is 2, the first wing must be 9. If it is 6, the second must be 9. Remove 9 from any other cell that sees both wings.
The pivot allows 1 or 2. If it is 1, the {1, 3} wing must be 3. If it is 2, the {2, 3} wing must be 3.

lessons.title: XYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: An XYZ-Wing has one cell with three candidates and two nearby cells with two each. Together they guarantee a place for one shared digit. Any other cell that sees all three loses that digit.

blocks.title: Look for a three-candidate pivot

paragraphs: Start with a pivot such as {2, 6, 9}. Look for two cells it sees with {2, 9} and {6, 9}.
If the pivot is 2 or 6, one wing must be 9. If the pivot is 9, the pivot itself supplies the 9. Remove 9 from any other cell that sees all three.
The pivot allows 2, 8, or 9. A 2 or 9 forces 8 into a wing. An 8 puts it in the pivot itself.
R6C5 sees the wing at R2C5 in column 5. It sees the pivot and the other wing in box 5, so R6C5 loses 8.

lessons.title: W-Wing
lessons.summary: A W-Wing connects two cells that share the same two candidates. A two-place link for one digit forces at least one of those cells to use the other digit. A cell that sees both cannot use it.

blocks.title: Connect two cells with the same pair

paragraphs: Find two cells with the same two candidates, such as {2, 7}. Find a house with just two places for 2. Each of those places must see a different one of your pair cells.
One of the two places in the house must be 2. It blocks 2 in the pair cell it sees, so that cell must be 7. Remove 7 from any other cell that sees both pair cells.
Both wings allow 5 or 7. The only two places for 7 in column 2 each see a different wing. Whichever end is 7 forces its wing to be 5.

lessons.title: Jellyfish
lessons.summary: A Jellyfish reserves four columns for one digit. If four rows can place their copies only in those columns, each column gets one. The digit cannot go elsewhere in those columns.

blocks.title: Count the columns across four rows

paragraphs: Choose a digit. Start with rows that each have a few places for it. Look for four rows whose candidates together use just four columns.
Each of the four rows needs one copy in a different column. Remove that digit from those columns outside the four rows. You can also start with four columns.

blocks.title: Finned Jellyfish

paragraphs: For a finned Jellyfish, find the extra candidates outside the four covers. All must share a box. Look in that box, on a cover line outside the base lines.
If any fin is true, the box rules out the target. If all fins are false, the four base lines need all four covers.

blocks.title: Sashimi Jellyfish

paragraphs: In a sashimi Jellyfish, at least one base line has just one candidate left without its fins. It uses one cover, and each remaining line needs a different cover. Look for removals in the fin box.

lessons.title: The uniqueness assumption
lessons.summary: Some techniques depend on the puzzle having exactly one solution. If an arrangement would let you swap digits to produce a second solution, that arrangement cannot occur in a puzzle known to have just one.

blocks.title: Look for a swap that preserves every house

paragraphs: Use a uniqueness technique only on a puzzle known to have exactly one solution.

blocks.title: Why a second completion matters

paragraphs: Consider R1C2, R1C3, R4C2, and R4C3 in a classic puzzle. Suppose all four began empty and the solution fills them with alternating 1s and 7s.
Swap the 1s and 7s in those four cells. Each affected row, column, and box still has one of each. That gives a second solution.

blocks.caption: The same four cells before and after the swap

blocks.title: Know when this argument applies

paragraphs: Unique Rectangles and BUG use this argument. Givens must stay in place, and the swap must respect every rule of the puzzle. A rectangle in four boxes or an extra variant clue can prevent the swap.
For an imported puzzle, finding one solution alone does not establish uniqueness.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: A solver stops after finding one solution. Has it proved the puzzle has only one?
questions.explanation: Another solution can still exist. The solver must also rule out a second one.

questions.prompt: Can you use an ordinary candidate conflict without knowing whether the puzzle has one solution?
questions.explanation: Every solution must obey the same row, column, and box rules.

questions.prompt: Can a swap that changes a given prove a second solution?
questions.explanation: A solution must keep every given in its original cell.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle
lessons.summary: Four cells in two rows, two columns, and two boxes can form a Unique Rectangle. If they held only the same two digits, swapping the diagonals would give another solution. A puzzle with one solution needs an extra digit in at least one corner.

blocks.title: Check the four corners and their boxes

paragraphs: Start with a classic puzzle known to have one solution. Find four empty corners in two rows, two columns, and exactly two boxes. Look for the same two candidates in all four.
If the corners use only those digits, each diagonal holds one digit. Swapping the diagonals preserves both rows, both columns, and both boxes. At least one corner must use a different digit.

blocks.title: Type 1 with extras in one corner

paragraphs: If three corners allow only the pair, the fourth must use an extra digit. Remove both digits of the pair from that corner.

blocks.title: Type 2 with the same extra on adjacent corners

paragraphs: If two adjacent corners have the same single extra digit, one of them must use it. The other two corners must have only the pair. Remove the extra digit from any other cell that sees both possible places.

blocks.title: Type 3 with a subset of extra digits

paragraphs: Two adjacent corners can have several extras. Together they need at least one of them. Count those corners as one slot in a house they share.
Add other cells in that house. If the different extras and those cells’ candidates match the number of slots, those digits fill the slots. Remove them elsewhere in the house.

blocks.title: Type 4 with a strong link on one side

paragraphs: Suppose the two corners with extras are the only places in their shared house for one digit of the pair. One of those corners must use it. If the other uses the second digit, the four corners can swap. Remove the second digit from both corners with extras.

blocks.title: Type 5 with the same extra across the diagonals

paragraphs: Look for the same single extra digit in two opposite corners or in three corners. If all other candidates belong to the pair, at least one corner must use the extra. Remove it from any other cell that sees every possible copy.

blocks.title: Type 6 with one digit locked to a diagonal

paragraphs: Two opposite corners have extras. Look for one digit of the pair confined to the rectangle in both rows and both columns. That digit must fill a diagonal.
If it fills the diagonal with extras, the opposite corners must use the other digit. The swap is then possible. Remove the linked digit from the corners with extras.

blocks.title: Hidden Rectangle

paragraphs: Start at a corner with only the pair. At the opposite corner, find a digit confined to the rectangle in both its row and its column. Filling that corner with the other digit forces the swap. Remove that other digit there.

blocks.title: Avoidable rectangles

paragraphs: An avoidable rectangle can include digits you placed after the puzzle began. All four corners must have started empty. With three filled corners, remove the candidate that completes the swap.
With two filled corners and the same single extra in both empty corners, one of the extras must be true. Remove it from other cells that see both.

blocks.title: When earlier moves removed candidates

paragraphs: Earlier moves can remove a rectangle digit from your notes. For this version, use the givens to check that both swapped fillings are possible in all four corners.

lessons.title: BUG+1
lessons.summary: In a BUG+1, removing one candidate leaves a grid whose remaining choices come in interchangeable pairs. Any solution of that reduced grid has a partner. A puzzle with exactly one solution must use the extra candidate.

blocks.title: Find the cell with three candidates

paragraphs: Look for one empty cell with three candidates and exactly two candidates in every other empty cell.
In the three-candidate cell, find the digit with three possible places in its row, three in its column, and three in its box.
Imagine removing that digit. Every empty cell must now have two candidates. In each row, column, and box, every missing digit must have exactly two possible places.

If those counts hold across the grid, the removal leaves a Bivalue Universal Grave (BUG). Switching every originally empty cell to its other choice turns any solution of that grid into a second one. Place the extra digit in the three-candidate cell.

groups.title: Very Hard
groups.overview: Connect pairs of candidates with chains and colors.

lessons.title: Following a chain
lessons.summary: A chain follows what one candidate implies about the next. It can show that at least one of two distant candidates is true. Anything that conflicts with both can then be ruled out.

blocks.title: Read a chain from one end

paragraphs: Find a strong link between two candidates. From its far end, look for a weak link to another candidate that has a strong link.

blocks.title: One forced step at a time

paragraphs: Call the four candidates A, B, C, and D. The example connects them in this order with a strong link, a weak link, and a strong link.

blocks.caption: What follows if A is false

paragraphs: Suppose A is false. The links force B true, C false, and D true. Either A is true or D must be true. You can remove any candidate that conflicts with both.
The two ends can both be true. A chain like this only rules out the case where both are false.

blocks.title: Colors record a relationship

paragraphs: Two colors can mark opposite choices along links where exactly one end is true. A weak link alone permits both ends to be false, so it cannot establish opposite colors.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: One end of a link is false. Which type of link can force the other end true?
questions.explanation: A strong link needs at least one true end.

questions.prompt: At least one end of a chain is true. Which candidate does that rule out?
options: A candidate conflicting with both ends
questions.explanation: A candidate that conflicts with both ends leaves neither end able to be true.

questions.prompt: Can you assume the ends of any weak link have opposite states?
questions.explanation: Both ends can be false. To give the two ends opposite colors, exactly one must be true.

lessons.title: Why two colors work
lessons.summary: When exactly one of two candidates is true, opposite colors can mark the two choices. Connected pairs carry those colors across the grid. Within one connected group, all candidates of the correct color are true together.

blocks.title: Find a pair with exactly one true end

paragraphs: Choose a house with two possible places for a digit. Color one blue and one amber.

blocks.title: Each pair has exactly one true candidate

paragraphs: Exactly one of those places must hold the digit. This pair has both a strong and a weak link. From either end, find another such pair. Give its new end the opposite color.

blocks.title: Test what each color means

paragraphs: Within one connected set, either all blue candidates are true or all amber candidates are true. If two blue candidates conflict, remove blue throughout that set.
A candidate that conflicts with both colors also has to go. Keep disconnected sets separate. Blue in one set can mean something different from blue in another.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Can you use a weak link alone to assign opposite colors to its ends?
questions.explanation: A weak link can have two false ends. Opposite colors mean exactly one end is true.

questions.prompt: An uncolored 5 sees a blue 5 and an amber 5 in one connected set. Which 5 can you remove?
questions.explanation: Either blue or amber supplies a 5 that rules out the uncolored one.

questions.prompt: Two blue candidates in different sets conflict. Can you remove blue from both sets?
questions.explanation: The two sets choose their true colors independently. The conflict only rules out blue in both at once.

lessons.title: Simple Coloring
lessons.summary: Simple Coloring follows one digit through houses with exactly two places for it. Within a connected group, one color marks the digit’s true positions. An uncolored candidate that sees a copy of each color cannot hold the digit.

blocks.title: Follow pairs for one digit

paragraphs: Highlight a digit. In a house with exactly two places for it, color one place blue and the other amber.
At each colored cell, look for another house with exactly two places for that digit. Give the new cell the opposite color. Continue until you find no more connected pairs.

blocks.title: Color trap

paragraphs: If an uncolored candidate sees both a blue and an amber candidate, remove it. Whichever color holds the digit rules it out.

blocks.title: Color wrap

paragraphs: If two blue candidates see each other, blue cannot be true in this set. Remove every blue candidate in the set. Its amber candidates must be true.

blocks.title: No place for the digit

paragraphs: Suppose one color is true. If that leaves any house without a place for the digit, remove that color throughout the set.

lessons.title: X-Chain
lessons.summary: An X-Chain follows a single digit through alternating strong and weak links. With a strong link at each end, at least one end holds the digit. Any other cell that sees both ends loses that candidate.

blocks.title: Connect two-place links for one digit

paragraphs: Highlight a digit. Find a house where it has only two places. From one end of that pair, find another possible place that it sees.
The first pair has a strong link. If one end is false, its partner must be true. Two candidates for the same digit that see each other have a weak link.

Alternate strong and weak links and finish with a strong link. Suppose the starting candidate is false. The first link forces its partner, and the next rules out its neighbor. Continue to the far end, which must then be true.
At least one end contains the digit. Remove it from any other cell that sees both ends. A Skyscraper and a Two-String Kite are short examples of this chain.

lessons.title: XY-Chain
lessons.summary: An XY-Chain passes from one two-candidate cell to the next through a digit they share. When both ends point to the same digit, at least one end must hold it. A cell that sees both ends cannot hold it.

blocks.title: Connect cells with two candidates each

paragraphs: Choose a cell with two candidates. Suppose one digit is false. Its other digit must then be true.
Find a two-candidate cell that sees the first and shares that forced digit. The shared digit is false in the new cell, so its other digit must be true. Repeat through the chain.

Stop when the forced digit in the last cell matches the digit you first supposed false. One end must contain that digit. Remove it from other cells that see both ends. An XY-Wing uses three cells this way.

lessons.title: 3D Medusa
lessons.summary: 3D Medusa uses two colors to track candidates for several digits. Within one connected group, either all the blue candidates or all the amber candidates are true. If two blue 7s share a row, blue is impossible throughout that group.

blocks.title: Build a group from linked pairs

paragraphs: Find a cell with exactly two candidates, such as 2 and 7. Color the 2 blue and the 7 amber. If its row has just one other place for 7, color that 7 blue.

Continue from each colored candidate. In a two-candidate cell, give the other digit the opposite color. In a row, column, or box with just two places for the same digit, give its other place the opposite color.

blocks.title: When one color breaks a rule

items: One color puts two digits in one cell.
One color puts the same digit twice in a house.
One color leaves an empty cell with no candidates.
One color leaves a house with no place for a missing digit.

paragraphs: If a color causes one of these conflicts, remove every candidate of that color in this set. Place the candidates of the other color.

blocks.title: When either color rules out the same candidate

items: If a cell contains both colors, either color fills it. Remove its uncolored candidates.
If an uncolored 5 sees both a blue 5 and an amber 5, remove the uncolored 5.
If one color fills the cell and the other places its candidate digit in a peer, both colors rule out that candidate.

lessons.title: Almost locked set basics
lessons.summary: Two cells in one house with three candidate digits between them form an almost locked set. The cells need two different digits, so they can leave out only one. Larger sets follow the same counting rule.

blocks.title: Count the digits in cells that share a house

paragraphs: Choose a few empty cells in the same row, column, or box. Count the different digits across all their candidate lists.

blocks.title: One extra digit

paragraphs: An almost locked set (ALS) has exactly one more possible digit than cells. For example, {1, 4} and {4, 8} give two cells three possible digits. One cell with two candidates is the smallest ALS.

blocks.caption: What the two cells must use

paragraphs: The two cells must use different digits, so exactly one of the three digits is absent. If the set loses every possible 4, the cells must use 1 and 8.

blocks.title: An ALS alone does not remove anything

paragraphs: The count alone cannot tell you which digit is absent. A link to another cell or set can rule out one digit and force all the others.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Two cells in a row allow {1, 4} and {4, 8}. Do they form an ALS?
questions.explanation: They share a row and have three different digits for two cells.

questions.prompt: Does finding an ALS by itself let you remove one of its digits from nearby cells?
questions.explanation: The set can omit one digit. You need a reason it must use the digit you want to remove elsewhere.

questions.prompt: How many different candidate digits does a three-cell ALS have?
questions.explanation: An ALS has one more digit than cells, so three cells need four digits.

lessons.title: WXYZ-Wing
lessons.summary: A WXYZ-Wing has four cells with four candidate digits between them. If three of those digits can each appear only once, the four cells must include the fourth digit. That can rule it out in nearby cells.

blocks.title: Count the digits that can repeat

paragraphs: Find four cells with just four different candidate digits between them. For each digit, see whether every pair of cells with that digit shares a row, column, or box.
If every pair sees each other, that digit can occur only once in the four cells. At least three digits must pass this test.

blocks.title: When only one digit can repeat

paragraphs: Those three digits can fill at most three cells. The fourth digit must appear somewhere in the wing. Remove it from any outside cell that sees every possible copy in the wing.

notes.title: Read this example as ALS-XZ
paragraphs: R4C3, R4C4, and R4C6 share row 4. Their four possible digits are 1, 2, 5, and 9. R6C1 forms a second set with {1, 9}.
All possible 1s in the two sets lie in box 4. At least one set must omit 1 and use its other digits, including 9.
A 9 in R4C2 blocks the row set through row 4. It also blocks the 9 in R6C1 through box 4. Remove 9 from R4C2.

blocks.title: When no digit can repeat

paragraphs: If all four digits can occur only once, the wing must contain each one. For each digit, look for an outside cell that sees every possible copy inside.

blocks.title: The almost locked set connection

paragraphs: An almost locked set has one more possible digit than cells, all in one house. Some WXYZ-Wings split into two such sets and also have an ALS-XZ proof.

references.label: Almost Locked Sets (ALS): the shared idea

lessons.title: Unique Loop
lessons.summary: A Unique Loop extends the idea of a Unique Rectangle around a ring. If the ring used only its two shared digits, swapping them would preserve every affected house. In a puzzle with one solution, at least one ring cell needs an extra digit.

blocks.title: Trace the same two digits around a ring

paragraphs: In a puzzle with one solution, follow the same two candidate digits around a ring of empty cells. Each house that meets the ring must contain exactly two ring cells, one on each side of the swap.
If the ring uses only those two digits, swapping them gives a second solution. At least one cell must use an extra digit.

copy.description: The loop alternates between 1 and 6. Only R6C4 allows another digit, 5. Removing 1 and 6 there prevents the swap.

guide.start: In a puzzle with one solution, follow the same two candidate digits around a ring of empty cells.
guide.check: Each house that meets the ring must contain exactly two ring cells, one on each side of the swap.
guide.reason: If the ring uses only those two digits, swapping them gives a second solution. At least one cell must use an extra digit.

groups.title: Expert
groups.overview: Alternate strong and weak links in chains and loops.

lessons.title: Reading chain notation
lessons.summary: Chain notation records a sequence of candidate choices. Each symbol tells you whether ruling out one choice forces the next, or whether placing one rules out the next. The two ends tell you which deduction the chain supports.

blocks.title: Read the two sides of each link

paragraphs: Read the candidate on each side of a symbol. The equals sign marks a strong link. A dash marks a weak link.

blocks.caption: How to read the symbols
rows: A and B have a strong link.
A and B have a weak link.
A strong link between 2 and 7 inside R6C4.

blocks.title: Read the implications, not just the symbols

paragraphs: In A = B - C = D, suppose A is false. The strong link forces B true. The weak link makes C false, so the last strong link forces D true.
A pair can have both kinds of link. The symbol tells you which property the proof uses here.

blocks.title: Check the ends separately

paragraphs: Look at the digits as well as the cells at the two ends. A chain can switch digits in the middle. A removal must conflict with both endpoint candidates.
If the path returns to its starting candidate, compare the first and last links at that point.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Does A = B mean that A and B are both true or both false?
questions.explanation: The equals sign marks a strong link. At least one end must be true.

questions.prompt: Can a dash represent a pair that has both a strong and a weak link?
questions.explanation: The dash uses the weak link. It shows that the two ends cannot both be true.

questions.prompt: Is a chain invalid just because it switches digits inside a cell?
questions.explanation: A chain can switch digits. Each step must still have the strong or weak link it uses.

references.label: Pure Sudoku: propositions and inference chains

lessons.title: Alternating Inference Chains
lessons.summary: An alternating inference chain (AIC) joins strong and weak links in turn. With strong links at both ends, ruling out the first end forces the last. A candidate that conflicts with both ends cannot be true.

blocks.title: Start from a strong link

paragraphs: Begin with a two-candidate cell or the only two places for a digit in a house. Both give a strong link. From the far end, find a conflict that leads to another strong link.

An alternating inference chain (AIC) starts and ends with a strong link for this deduction. If the first end is false, the links force the last end true. Any candidate that rules out both ends is impossible.

blocks.title: Type 1 with the same digit at both ends

paragraphs: If both ends are 4, remove 4 from any other cell that sees both. The middle of the chain can use other digits.

blocks.title: Type 2 with different digits

paragraphs: Suppose the ends are 2 in A and 7 in B, and the cells share a house. A 7 in A rules out 2 in A and 7 in B. Remove 7 from A. The same argument removes 2 from B if it is a candidate there.

lessons.title: When a chain closes
lessons.summary: A chain can return to the candidate where it began. The two links that meet there determine what the loop proves. They can settle that candidate or show where other candidates conflict with the loop.

blocks.title: Check the links at the join

paragraphs: Follow the chain back to its starting candidate. Look at the two links that meet there.

blocks.title: Two matching links force the starting candidate

paragraphs: If both links are weak, suppose the candidate is true. The loop forces it false, so remove it. If both links are strong, suppose it is false. The loop forces it true, so place it.

blocks.title: An alternating join strengthens each weak link

paragraphs: If the links alternate even at the join, choose any weak link. Follow the rest of the loop between its ends. That path starts and ends with strong links, so at least one end is true.
The weak link prevents both ends from being true. Remove any candidate that conflicts with both. Other weak links can give other removals.

blocks.caption: What happens where the loop closes
rows: Exactly one end of each weak link is true.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Two weak links meet at the starting candidate. Which assumption about that candidate leads to a conflict?
questions.explanation: If the candidate starts true, the first weak link rules out its neighbor. The loop returns and rules out the starting candidate.

questions.prompt: A loop alternates at every join. Why does it rule out a candidate that conflicts with both ends of one weak link?
options: At least one of those endpoints must be true
questions.explanation: Go around the rest of the loop. If one end is false, that path forces the other end true.

lessons.title: Nice Loops
lessons.summary: A Nice Loop follows candidate links back to the starting choice. A break in the alternation at that choice can force or exclude it. When the links alternate all the way around, a weak link must have one true end.

blocks.title: Trace the chain back to its start

paragraphs: Start at a candidate with a strong link and a weak link. A two-candidate cell in a house with a two-place digit is a good place to look.
Trace alternating links until you return to the first candidate. The move depends on the two links that meet there.

blocks.title: Discontinuous Nice Loop

paragraphs: With two weak links at the join, assuming the candidate is true leads back to false. Remove it. With two strong links, assuming it is false leads back to true. Place it.

blocks.title: Continuous Nice Loop

paragraphs: If the links alternate all the way around, pick a weak link. The rest of the loop forces one of its ends to be true. Remove any candidate that conflicts with both ends of that link.

groups.title: Master
groups.overview: Build chains that include groups of candidates or almost locked sets.

lessons.title: Grouped candidates
lessons.summary: Several candidates can stand for one claim, such as “one of these two cells is 5.” The claim can serve as one end of a link. To rule it out, you must rule out every member.

blocks.title: Group the places where a line crosses a box

paragraphs: Find two or three possible places for one digit where a row or column crosses a box.

blocks.title: A group is one statement

paragraphs: Let G mean “5 is in R3C1 or R3C2.” If either cell is 5, G is true. To rule out G, you must rule out both places.
Suppose row 3 allows 5 only in those two cells and R3C8. The row needs a 5, so G and the 5 in R3C8 have a strong link.

blocks.title: Check every member

paragraphs: An outside candidate conflicts with G only if it rules out every member. Use the same test at a grouped chain end. A target must conflict with every candidate at both ends.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: G means “R3C1 or R3C2 is 5.” If only R3C1 loses 5, is G false?
questions.explanation: R3C2 can still be 5.

questions.prompt: An outside candidate sees only one of two possible 5s in a group. Does that prove a weak link to the group?
questions.explanation: The other 5 can still make the group true.

questions.prompt: A group and one other cell cover every possible 5 in a row. Do they have a strong link?
questions.explanation: The row needs one 5. If the group has none, the other cell must be 5.

references.label: Sudoku Coach: AICs and grouped candidates
Pure Sudoku: propositions and inference chains

lessons.title: Grouped AIC
lessons.summary: A grouped AIC lets several places for one digit act as a single end of a link. This extends a chain through a house where neither cell alone supplies the link. An outside candidate must conflict with the whole group to rule it out.

blocks.title: Find a group that shares a link

paragraphs: Find a group of possible places for one digit where a line crosses a box. Read it as one claim that at least one of those cells holds the digit.

blocks.title: Grouped AIC

paragraphs: If the group and another choice cover every place for the digit in a house, they have a strong link. A weak link to the group must rule out every member.
Alternate the links as in an AIC. A candidate that conflicts with every choice at both ends can be removed.

lessons.title: Grouped Nice Loops
lessons.summary: A grouped Nice Loop closes a chain through a group of possible places for one digit. A true group needs at least one of its members. A false group rules out all of them.

blocks.title: Follow a grouped link back to the start

paragraphs: Start with a group of places for one digit. Follow alternating links back to the starting choice. Check the two links at the join.

blocks.title: Grouped Discontinuous Nice Loop

paragraphs: If both links at a single starting candidate are weak, the loop rules it out. If both are strong, it forces the candidate. Inside the loop, a false group means every member is false.

blocks.title: Grouped Continuous Nice Loop

paragraphs: If the links alternate around the whole loop, each weak link needs one true end. To remove a candidate, it must rule out every possible member at both ends of that link.

lessons.title: Restricted common candidates
lessons.summary: Two almost locked sets can share a candidate digit that only one of them can use. This is a restricted common candidate. At least one set must leave it out and use all its other digits.

blocks.title: Compare every place for the shared digit

paragraphs: Choose two separate almost locked sets with no cells in common. Pick a digit that appears in both.

blocks.title: Shared is not yet restricted

paragraphs: Compare every place for that digit in the first set with every place in the second. If every cross-set pair sees each other, the digit is a restricted common candidate (RCC).
For example, if every possible 6 in both sets lies in row 8, only one set can use 6.

blocks.caption: Does 6 link these sets?
rows: All occurrences in both sets share row 8
One occurrence in the first set cannot see one in the second
Both sets contain 6, but their cells have no shared house

blocks.title: Why the connection matters

paragraphs: If the first set uses 6, the second loses every 6. It must use all its remaining digits. The first set is also free to omit 6. If neither set uses it, both sets use all their other digits.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Both sets include 6. One possible 6 misses a 6 in the other set. Is 6 a restricted common candidate?
questions.explanation: Every possible 6 in one set must see every possible 6 in the other.

questions.prompt: Must exactly one set use the restricted common digit?
questions.explanation: At most one set can use the digit. Both can omit it.

questions.prompt: One set uses the restricted common digit. What happens to the other set?
options: It loses that digit and becomes locked
It must use that digit too
questions.explanation: Every copy in the other set conflicts with that digit. The other set must use all its remaining digits.

lessons.title: Links inside an almost locked set
lessons.summary: An almost locked set can omit only one of its candidate digits. If it omits 4, for example, it must use every other digit in its list. That relationship supplies a strong link between two different digits.

blocks.title: Choose two digits in one set

paragraphs: Find an almost locked set. Choose two of its different digits. Mark every place for each digit inside the set.

blocks.title: The set can omit only one digit

paragraphs: Suppose two cells in one row allow {1, 4} and {4, 8}. They need two different digits. If both 4s are false, the cells must use 1 and 8.
The set can miss only one digit. “The set uses 1” and “the set uses 4” have a strong link. Both statements can be true.

blocks.title: Connect to the whole digit group

paragraphs: To rule out 4 throughout the set, an outside 4 must see every 4 inside. If that happens, the set must use 1. That in turn rules out an outside 1 that sees every possible 1 inside.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: An outside 4 sees only one of two 4s in a set. Does it rule out 4 throughout the set?
questions.explanation: The second possible 4 remains. An outside digit must see both places to rule out the whole group.

questions.prompt: Can this set use both 1 and 4 despite the strong link between them?
questions.explanation: The set can use 1 and 4 and omit 8. A strong link allows both ends to be true.

references.label: HoDoKu on ALS links in chains

lessons.title: Almost Locked Sets (ALS)
lessons.summary: An almost locked set has one more possible digit than cells, all in one house. Losing one digit forces the set to use every other digit. Two sets can pass that restriction between them through a shared candidate.

blocks.title: Find two sets with a shared digit

paragraphs: Find two almost locked sets near each other. Start with a two-candidate cell or two cells in one house with three different candidates.
An almost locked set (ALS) has one more candidate digit than cells. All its cells share a house, so they must use different digits. The set can omit exactly one digit from its combined list.

blocks.title: One digit short of a locked subset

paragraphs: Two cells with {1, 2} and {2, 3} form an ALS. If the set loses 1, the first cell must be 2 and the second must be 3. Those two digits now fill the set.

blocks.title: ALS-XZ: connect two sets

paragraphs: Choose a shared digit X. Every X in the first set must see every X in the second. At least one set must then omit X and use every other digit.
If the sets also share Z, one set must use Z. Remove Z from any outside cell that sees every possible Z in both sets.

notes.title: The shared digits in this example
paragraphs: R3C7 and R5C7 allow three digits between them, 1, 3, and 4. R2C4, R2C5, R2C7, and R2C9 allow five digits, 1, 3, 4, 5, and 9.
The 3s in both sets share column 7. At least one set must omit 3, so it must use its other digits, including 1.
R2C8 sees every possible 1 in both sets. Remove 1 from R2C8.

blocks.title: Named patterns in the ALS family

items: ALS-XZ links two sets through a restricted common candidate.
Some WXYZ-Wings split into two linked sets with four cells in total.
An ALS-XY-Wing links three sets through two different restricted common candidates.
In an ALS Chain, each middle set uses a different digit for each of its two links.

paragraphs: In a chain of sets, a digit forced into one set can rule it out in the next. The named patterns use different numbers of sets or links.

blocks.title: Try an ALS pattern

lessons.title: Death Blossom
lessons.summary: A Death Blossom starts from one cell with several possible digits. Each choice forces a different almost locked set to use the same shared digit. A cell that sees every possible copy in those sets cannot use it.

blocks.title: Find a set for each choice in the stem cell

paragraphs: Choose a cell with a short candidate list. This is the stem. For each stem digit, find an almost locked set that contains it. The stem must see every copy of that digit in its set.
Each set is a petal. If the stem is 5, its petal loses every 5 and must use all its other digits.
Find a different digit shared by every petal. Whichever digit fills the stem, one petal must use that shared digit. Remove it from an outside cell only if it sees every possible copy in every petal.

copy.description: R6C9 allows 1, 5, or 7. The 1 petal uses R8C1, R8C2, R8C3, and R8C9. The 5 petal uses R4C4 and R6C6. The 7 petal uses R4C4 and R6C4. Each petal contains a possible 3.

guide.start: Find the stem cell. Which almost locked set does each stem digit reach?
guide.check: For each stem digit, look for every copy in its petal. They must all see the stem.
guide.reason: Each stem choice forces the shared digit into its petal. An outside candidate that sees every possible copy in every petal loses that digit.

lessons.title: Sue de Coq
lessons.summary: In Sue de Coq, a line and a box share cells that must draw from two separate groups of digits. Together the overlap and its neighbors use up those groups. That rules out digits elsewhere in the line or box.

blocks.title: Count the cells where a line crosses a box

paragraphs: Find two or three empty cells where a line crosses a box. Count the digits those cells can use. Look for one set in the rest of the line and another in the rest of the box. Their digits must be separate.
The side sets must account for all the extra choices in the overlap. Together with the overlap, each set needs all its digits inside its own house. Remove those digits elsewhere in that house.

copy.description: R7C1 and R7C3 lie in both row 7 and box 7. Compare their candidates with R7C5 and R7C7 in the row and R8C3 in the box.

guide.start: Find two or three empty cells where a line crosses a box. Count the digits those cells can use.
guide.check: Look for one set in the rest of the line and another in the rest of the box. Their digits must be separate.
guide.reason: The side sets must account for all the extra choices in the overlap. Together with the overlap, each set needs all its digits inside its own house. Remove those digits elsewhere in that house.

lessons.title: ALS alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: An almost locked set can miss only one of its digits. That makes any two different digits in the set a strong link. An alternating chain can use this link even when each digit has several possible cells.

blocks.title: Link two digits through an almost locked set

paragraphs: Find an almost locked set. Pick two different digits and mark every place for each digit inside it. If the set misses either digit, it must use the other. Use that strong link in a chain. An outside weak link must see every copy of the digit it rules out.
With strong links at both ends, ruling out the first end forces the last. Remove a candidate that conflicts with every possibility at both ends.

copy.description: Read each group in the set as one choice. Follow the solid link between the two groups, then continue along the chain.

guide.start: Find an almost locked set. Pick two different digits and mark every place for each digit inside it.
guide.check: If the set misses either digit, it must use the other. Use that strong link in a chain. An outside weak link must see every copy of the digit it rules out.
guide.reason: With strong links at both ends, ruling out the first end forces the last. Remove a candidate that conflicts with every possibility at both ends.

lessons.title: ALS discontinuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: An almost locked set can provide the strong link that closes a loop. If two weak links meet at the starting candidate, the loop rules it out. If two strong links meet there, the loop forces it.

blocks.title: Trace the loop to a candidate with matching links

paragraphs: Find two digits in an almost locked set. At least one must appear. Use that strong link in an alternating chain. Follow the chain back to a single candidate. Look at the two links that meet there.
With two weak links at the join, assuming the candidate is true rules it out. With two strong links, assuming it is false forces it.

copy.description: Start where the two links match. Follow each group through the set and back to the starting candidate.

guide.start: Find two digits in an almost locked set. At least one must appear. Use that strong link in an alternating chain.
guide.check: Follow the chain back to a single candidate. Look at the two links that meet there.
guide.reason: With two weak links at the join, assuming the candidate is true rules it out. With two strong links, assuming it is false forces it.

lessons.title: ALS continuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: Two digits in an almost locked set can connect the ends of a continuous loop. The rest of the loop then needs one end of each weak link to be true. A candidate that rules out both ends is impossible.

blocks.title: Find a loop that alternates at the join

paragraphs: Use two digits of an almost locked set as the ends of a strong link. Follow alternating links until they return to the start. Make sure the links also alternate at the join. Choose a weak link and trace the rest of the loop between its ends.
The rest of the loop forces at least one end of the weak link to be true. A candidate that rules out both ends is impossible. The loop can also force other digits into the set.

copy.description: Match a crossed-out candidate to the link it blocks or the digit the set must use.

guide.start: Use two digits of an almost locked set as the ends of a strong link. Follow alternating links until they return to the start.
guide.check: Make sure the links also alternate at the join. Choose a weak link and trace the rest of the loop between its ends.
guide.reason: The rest of the loop forces at least one end of the weak link to be true. A candidate that rules out both ends is impossible. The loop can also force other digits into the set.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: In a puzzle with one solution, at least one corner of a Unique Rectangle must use an extra digit. Splitting the extra candidates into two groups gives a chain a strong link. At least one of those groups must be true.

blocks.title: Group the extra candidates at the four corners

paragraphs: In a puzzle with one solution, find four empty rectangle corners across exactly two boxes. Find the two digits common to all four corners. Group all the extra candidates into two choices. If neither group supplies a digit, the four corners can swap. Use the strong link between the groups.
The rectangle needs at least one extra digit. With a strong link at each end of the chain, at least one end must be true. Remove a candidate that conflicts with both ends.

copy.description: Trace the chain through the extra candidates. Together the two groups cover every way the rectangle can avoid the swap.

guide.start: In a puzzle with one solution, find four empty rectangle corners across exactly two boxes. Find the two digits common to all four corners.
guide.check: Group all the extra candidates into two choices. If neither group supplies a digit, the four corners can swap. Use the strong link between the groups.
guide.reason: The rectangle needs at least one extra digit. With a strong link at each end of the chain, at least one end must be true. Remove a candidate that conflicts with both ends.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle discontinuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: In a puzzle with one solution, a Unique Rectangle needs at least one extra digit. A loop can use that fact to return to its starting candidate and prove that it must be true or must be false.

blocks.title: Follow the rectangle link back to one candidate

paragraphs: In a puzzle with one solution, find a Unique Rectangle in two boxes. Divide its extra candidates into two groups. Use the groups as the ends of a strong link. Follow alternating links back to one candidate where the first and last links match.
Two weak links at the join rule out that candidate. Two strong links force it. In either case, assuming the opposite makes the loop contradict itself.

copy.description: Here two strong links meet. If the candidate at the join is false, following the loop forces it true.

guide.start: In a puzzle with one solution, find a Unique Rectangle in two boxes. Divide its extra candidates into two groups.
guide.check: Use the groups as the ends of a strong link. Follow alternating links back to one candidate where the first and last links match.
guide.reason: Two weak links at the join rule out that candidate. Two strong links force it. In either case, assuming the opposite makes the loop contradict itself.

lessons.title: Unique Rectangle continuous Nice Loop
lessons.summary: A Unique Rectangle can supply a strong link in a puzzle with one solution. If a loop uses that link and alternates all the way around, each weak link needs a true end. An outside candidate that conflicts with both ends is impossible.

blocks.title: Check the weak links around the rectangle loop

paragraphs: In a puzzle with one solution, find a Unique Rectangle. Its extra candidates must include at least one true choice. Use that choice in a chain that alternates all the way around, including where the last link meets the first.
For any weak link, the rest of the loop forces one end true. Remove a candidate that rules out both ends. If an end is a group, it must rule out every member.

copy.description: Choose a weak link on the loop. Follow the other direction around the rectangle link to see why both ends cannot be false.

guide.start: In a puzzle with one solution, find a Unique Rectangle. Its extra candidates must include at least one true choice.
guide.check: Use that choice in a chain that alternates all the way around, including where the last link meets the first.
guide.reason: For any weak link, the rest of the loop forces one end true. Remove a candidate that rules out both ends. If an end is a group, it must rule out every member.

lessons.title: Fireworks
lessons.summary: A Firework uses a row and a column that cross inside a box. If neither line can place a digit outside the box, both need the same copy at their crossing. Each such digit needs the crossing cell or a place on a wing.

blocks.title: Find the pivot and its outside wings

paragraphs: Choose a cell as the pivot. For one digit, find all possible places along its row and column outside the pivot box. If neither outside wing holds that digit, the row and column both need it inside the box. Their only shared cell is the pivot.
Each Firework digit therefore needs a pivot or a wing. If the number of such digits matches the number of available cells, those cells must use all of them.

copy.description: The pivot is R1C9. Digits 1, 2, and 3 each need R1C9 or one of the two wings, R1C1 and R9C9. Those three digits fill all three cells.

guide.start: Choose a cell as the pivot. For one digit, find all possible places along its row and column outside the pivot box.
guide.check: If neither outside wing holds that digit, the row and column both need it inside the box. Their only shared cell is the pivot.
guide.reason: Each Firework digit therefore needs a pivot or a wing. If the number of such digits matches the number of available cells, those cells must use all of them.

lessons.title: Firework W-wing
lessons.summary: A Firework W-wing uses two outside cells with the same candidate pair. Blocking both Firework digits from their wings forces both into one pivot. That conflict rules out the placement that caused it.

blocks.title: Find two outside cells with the Firework pair

paragraphs: Find two Firework digits with the same pivot. Look for two cells outside the pattern that allow just those two digits. Try the target digit. Does it force the other digit into both two-candidate cells and block all wing places for both Firework digits?
If both Firework digits lose every wing place, both need the same pivot. A cell can contain only one digit, so remove the candidate that creates this conflict.

copy.description: Try 9 in R1C9. Follow the choices in R1C5 and R5C9 back to the pivot at R9C1.

guide.start: Find two Firework digits with the same pivot. Look for two cells outside the pattern that allow just those two digits.
guide.check: Try the target digit. Does it force the other digit into both two-candidate cells and block all wing places for both Firework digits?
guide.reason: If both Firework digits lose every wing place, both need the same pivot. A cell can contain only one digit, so remove the candidate that creates this conflict.

lessons.title: Firework L-wing
lessons.summary: A Firework L-wing connects a third digit to the two wings through a two-place link. If both wings held that third digit, two Firework digits would need the same pivot. The candidate that forces this conflict can be removed.

blocks.title: Link a third digit to the wings

paragraphs: Find two Firework digits with one wing cell on each arm. Look for a two-place link for a third digit, with one end at a wing. Trace the third digit from the opposite wing. Can it rule out the far end of the link and force the other wing to use that digit too?
If both wings use the third digit, neither can supply a Firework digit. Both Firework digits then need the pivot, so the starting candidate is impossible.

copy.description: Test 5 in R6C9. Row 1 has only two places for 5. Follow that pair to see what happens to the other wing.

guide.start: Find two Firework digits with one wing cell on each arm. Look for a two-place link for a third digit, with one end at a wing.
guide.check: Trace the third digit from the opposite wing. Can it rule out the far end of the link and force the other wing to use that digit too?
guide.reason: If both wings use the third digit, neither can supply a Firework digit. Both Firework digits then need the pivot, so the starting candidate is impossible.

lessons.title: Firework ALS-wing
lessons.summary: Two Fireworks can share a digit pair with a nearby two-candidate cell. Either choice in that cell forces both pivots to match it. A placement that conflicts with both possible arrangements is impossible.

blocks.title: Compare the two pivots with a two-candidate cell

paragraphs: Find two Fireworks with the same digit pair. Look for a cell with just that pair that sees all their outside wing places. Try each digit in that cell. For each choice, find the digit in both pivots. Where can the other digit go in each Firework?
Both choices force the pivots to use the same digit as the two-candidate cell. A candidate that fits neither choice can be removed.

copy.description: R5C5 allows 2 or 8. Try each there and follow it to both pivots, R1C9 and R9C1.

guide.start: Find two Fireworks with the same digit pair. Look for a cell with just that pair that sees all their outside wing places.
guide.check: Try each digit in that cell. For each choice, find the digit in both pivots. Where can the other digit go in each Firework?
guide.reason: Both choices force the pivots to use the same digit as the two-candidate cell. A candidate that fits neither choice can be removed.

lessons.title: Firework alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: A Firework digit must appear in its pivot or on a wing. Those places can supply a strong link for an alternating chain. The chain can then connect that digit to candidates outside the Firework.

blocks.title: Split the Firework places into two groups

paragraphs: Find a pivot and the possible wings for one Firework digit. Mark the places where that digit can go. Divide the places into two groups that cover every possibility. Link an outside candidate to a group only if it conflicts with every member.
The Firework needs at least one of the two groups. This supplies a strong link. If the whole chain starts and ends strong, a candidate cannot rule out both ends.

copy.description: Follow the chain through the pivot and wing groups. A true group needs at least one of its marked candidates.

guide.start: Find a pivot and the possible wings for one Firework digit. Mark the places where that digit can go.
guide.check: Divide the places into two groups that cover every possibility. Link an outside candidate to a group only if it conflicts with every member.
guide.reason: The Firework needs at least one of the two groups. This supplies a strong link. If the whole chain starts and ends strong, a candidate cannot rule out both ends.

lessons.title: Aligned Pair Exclusion
lessons.summary: Two cells can each have plausible candidates that fail when put together. If a digit in the first cell has no partner in the second, it cannot be the first cell’s digit.

blocks.title: Try the partners for a candidate

paragraphs: Choose two cells that see a common cell with few candidates. Hold one candidate fixed in the first cell. Try every candidate in the second cell. Look for a repeated digit in a house or a nearby cell with no candidate left.
If every pairing fails, remove the fixed candidate. One pairing without a conflict is enough to keep the candidate for this test.

copy.description: Suppose R1C4 is 5. Try each digit in R2C7. For each pair, look for a cell that loses its last candidate.

guide.start: Choose two cells that see a common cell with few candidates. Hold one candidate fixed in the first cell.
guide.check: Try every candidate in the second cell. Look for a repeated digit in a house or a nearby cell with no candidate left.
guide.reason: If every pairing fails, remove the fixed candidate. One pairing without a conflict is enough to keep the candidate for this test.

groups.title: Extreme
groups.overview: Follow trial moves and count how much room a digit has across several houses.

lessons.title: Assumptions and contradictions
lessons.summary: An assumption lets you examine what a candidate would force. A contradiction rules out that starting choice. A move that follows from every possible choice also holds on the original grid.

blocks.title: Follow one assumption on a trial grid

paragraphs: Choose one candidate. Suppose it is true or false. Keep the moves that follow under that assumption separate from the moves on your grid.

blocks.title: A contradiction must break a rule

paragraphs: An assumption fails if it leaves a cell empty of candidates or a house with no place for a required digit. It also fails if it forces conflicting placements. A pause in the solve proves nothing about the assumption.

blocks.caption: Two ways to finish a forcing proof
rows: If A breaks a Sudoku rule, A is false.
Every possible case leads to the same placement or removal.

blocks.title: Keep separate cases separate

paragraphs: If a cell allows {2, 5, 8}, examine all three cases before using a shared result. Never combine a removal from the 2 case with one from the 5 case.
Several moves within the same case can work together. A proof that combines them is called a forcing net.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: You try an assumption and cannot find another move. Have you ruled out the assumption?
questions.explanation: To rule it out, find a Sudoku rule that the assumption breaks.

questions.prompt: A cell allows 2, 5, or 8. Both 2 and 5 rule out a target 9. Is that enough to remove 9?
questions.explanation: The 8 case must also rule out 9, or it must lead to a contradiction.

questions.prompt: A trial rules out every possible 4 in row 7. What follows?
options: The row does not need a 4
questions.explanation: Row 7 needs a 4. An assumption that leaves it no place for 4 must be false.

lessons.title: Forcing Chains and Nets
lessons.summary: A forcing chain follows the consequences of a candidate. A forcing net combines several of those consequences. A contradiction disproves the starting choice, while a move shared by every possible choice holds on the original grid.

blocks.title: Trace the moves a candidate forces

paragraphs: Start with a cell with two candidates or a digit with two places in a house. Suppose one choice is true and look for a single it creates.
A placement rules out the other digits in its cell and the same digit in its peers. Follow each cell or house left with just one choice.

blocks.title: A choice breaks a rule

paragraphs: If a cell loses every candidate or a house loses every place for a digit, the assumption fails. A candidate that the chain both forces and rules out is also a contradiction. Reverse the starting assumption.

blocks.title: All choices lead to the same move

paragraphs: Try every candidate in one cell, every place for one digit in a house, or both states of one candidate. If all cases force the same move, you can make that move on the original grid.

blocks.title: Forcing nets

paragraphs: A forcing net can combine several changes from one assumption. For example, separate removals can leave a column with only one place for 5. Keep track of which removals force that placement.

lessons.title: Tridagon forcing net
lessons.summary: A Tridagon needs at least one candidate outside its three core digits. Each extra candidate is called a guardian. If every possible guardian rules out the same candidate elsewhere, that candidate cannot be true.

blocks.title: List the extra candidates in the Tridagon

paragraphs: Find a Tridagon and mark each candidate outside its three core digits. These extras are its guardians. At least one guardian must be true. Trace the moves each guardian forces, or test a choice that blocks them all.
If every guardian rules out the same candidate, remove it. A choice that leaves no possible guardian also fails.

copy.description: Start one branch for each guardian in the twelve cells. Compare the conclusions after all branches are complete.

guide.start: Find a Tridagon and mark each candidate outside its three core digits. These extras are its guardians.
guide.check: At least one guardian must be true. Trace the moves each guardian forces, or test a choice that blocks them all.
guide.reason: If every guardian rules out the same candidate, remove it. A choice that leaves no possible guardian also fails.

lessons.title: Dynamic forcing net
lessons.summary: In a dynamic forcing net, a trial move changes which links are available. A house with three places for a digit can have only two after a removal. The new link can carry the trial to a contradiction.

blocks.title: Find new links inside the trial

paragraphs: Choose a candidate and suppose it is true or false. Record the candidates that choice rules out. After each change, count the remaining places in the affected houses. Two places left for a digit can create a new strong link.
A link created under an assumption belongs to that case. If the changes leave a house without a required digit, the starting assumption fails.

copy.description: Follow the changes in order. Use each new link only after the earlier moves leave exactly two choices.

guide.start: Choose a candidate and suppose it is true or false. Record the candidates that choice rules out.
guide.check: After each change, count the remaining places in the affected houses. Two places left for a digit can create a new strong link.
guide.reason: A link created under an assumption belongs to that case. If the changes leave a house without a required digit, the starting assumption fails.

lessons.title: Advanced forcing net
lessons.summary: An advanced forcing net uses a solving technique inside a trial. For example, an assumption can create a pair that removes another candidate. The resulting moves belong to that trial until the proof settles the original choice.

blocks.title: Look for a technique inside the trial

paragraphs: Suppose a candidate is true or false. Follow the singles and removals that the assumption forces. On that trial grid, look for a subset, locked candidate, or another supported technique. Work out its move within the same case.
Every move in a branch depends on its starting choice. A contradiction rules out that choice. A move forced by every possible choice holds on the original grid.

copy.description: Read the candidate lists after each step. Which changes in this branch force the next move?

guide.start: Suppose a candidate is true or false. Follow the singles and removals that the assumption forces.
guide.check: On that trial grid, look for a subset, locked candidate, or another supported technique. Work out its move within the same case.
guide.reason: Every move in a branch depends on its starting choice. A contradiction rules out that choice. A move forced by every possible choice holds on the original grid.

lessons.title: Aligned Triplet Exclusion
lessons.summary: A candidate can fit with either of two cells separately and still fail when both cells need values. Aligned Triplet Exclusion rules out that candidate if every choice for the other two creates a conflict.

blocks.title: Test one candidate against two other cells

paragraphs: Choose three cells that affect nearby cells with short candidate lists. Pick a candidate in one of the three. Keep that candidate fixed. Try every combination for the other two cells. Check each for a repeated digit or an empty candidate list.
If every combination fails, the fixed digit cannot go in that cell. A failure for one combination alone rules out only that combination.

copy.description: Hold 4 in R1C4. Try all pairs of digits in the other two marked cells and find the conflict each pair causes.

guide.start: Choose three cells that affect nearby cells with short candidate lists. Pick a candidate in one of the three.
guide.check: Keep that candidate fixed. Try every combination for the other two cells. Check each for a repeated digit or an empty candidate list.
guide.reason: If every combination fails, the fixed digit cannot go in that cell. A failure for one combination alone rules out only that combination.

lessons.title: Tridagon
lessons.summary: A Tridagon has twelve cells in four boxes that cannot all be filled with just three core digits. At least one cell must use an extra candidate, called a guardian. A lone guardian must be true.

blocks.title: Find the core digits and their possible replacements

paragraphs: Choose four boxes across two bands and two stacks. In each box, mark three cells in different rows and columns. Each cell must allow at least two of the three core digits. Each triple must cover all three digits. Try the possible orders of the three digits in the first box. For each order, follow the row and column restrictions into the other boxes. In a Tridagon, every order ends in a conflict.
The core digits alone cannot fill the twelve cells. At least one extra candidate, called a guardian, must be true. If there is only one guardian, place it.

copy.description: Here the core digits are 2, 4, and 8. Only 6 in R6C3 can break the conflict.

guide.start: Choose four boxes across two bands and two stacks. In each box, mark three cells in different rows and columns. Each cell must allow at least two of the three core digits. Each triple must cover all three digits.
guide.check: Try the possible orders of the three digits in the first box. For each order, follow the row and column restrictions into the other boxes. In a Tridagon, every order ends in a conflict.
guide.reason: The core digits alone cannot fill the twelve cells. At least one extra candidate, called a guardian, must be true. If there is only one guardian, place it.

lessons.title: Tridagon alternating inference chain
lessons.summary: At least one guardian of a Tridagon must be true. Dividing all its guardians into two groups supplies a strong link for a chain. Either group can contain several possible candidates.

blocks.title: Group the guardians into two choices

paragraphs: Find a Tridagon with several extra candidates. List every guardian before you build the chain. Split the guardians into two groups. A candidate can rule out a group only if it conflicts with every guardian in it.
At least one guardian must be true, so the groups supply a strong link. An alternating chain with strong end links rules out any candidate that conflicts with both ends.

copy.description: Follow the link between the guardian groups. Check every member where a weak link meets a group.

guide.start: Find a Tridagon with several extra candidates. List every guardian before you build the chain.
guide.check: Split the guardians into two groups. A candidate can rule out a group only if it conflicts with every guardian in it.
guide.reason: At least one guardian must be true, so the groups supply a strong link. An alternating chain with strong end links rules out any candidate that conflicts with both ends.

lessons.title: Counting placements across houses
lessons.summary: A house has room for only one copy of a digit. Think of “5 in row 2” as one slot. When several cells need every slot on a list, no outside cell can use one of those slots.

blocks.title: Count the places available to a group of cells

paragraphs: Choose a group of cells. For each candidate, record a house and digit that can account for that placement. For example, a 1 in R2C1 can use the slot “1 in column 1.”

blocks.title: A slot is one digit in one house

paragraphs: A house can use a given digit only once. Each house and digit therefore supplies one slot. Include every candidate in the chosen cells.
If there are as many slots as cells, each cell must use exactly one. All the slots are necessary.

blocks.title: An overlap can use two slots

paragraphs: If the list includes both “1 in row 1” and “1 in column 1,” a 1 in R1C1 uses two slots. That leaves too few for the other cells. An outside cell also cannot use a slot that the group needs.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Four cells need all four available slots. Can one cell use two slots?
questions.explanation: That leaves only two slots for the three other cells.

questions.prompt: A candidate in one chosen cell uses none of the counted slots. Does the equal count still prove the removal?
questions.explanation: That candidate can fill a cell without using a slot. The count no longer covers every choice.

lessons.title: SK loop
lessons.summary: An SK loop links pairs of cells around four placed digits. When the ring has exactly enough places for its digits, it must use them all. An outside candidate that needs one of those places is impossible.

blocks.title: Find a ring around four givens

paragraphs: Find four givens at the corners of a rectangle. Look beside them for pairs of cells that share candidate digits around the ring. Count one slot for each linked digit in each house. Every candidate in the ring must use a slot, and the number of slots must equal the number of cells.
The ring needs every slot. An outside placement that uses a slot leaves too few for the ring. A candidate inside the ring that uses two slots also leaves too few.

copy.description: Follow the arms in order. Count a digit once per linked house before comparing the total with the number of ring cells.

guide.start: Find four givens at the corners of a rectangle. Look beside them for pairs of cells that share candidate digits around the ring.
guide.check: Count one slot for each linked digit in each house. Every candidate in the ring must use a slot, and the number of slots must equal the number of cells.
guide.reason: The ring needs every slot. An outside placement that uses a slot leaves too few for the ring. A candidate inside the ring that uses two slots also leaves too few.

lessons.title: Multi-sector locked sets
lessons.summary: A multi-sector locked set counts places for digits across several houses at once. When the cells need every available slot, a candidate cannot use a slot from outside the set or use two slots inside it.

blocks.title: Count the digit slots across the houses

paragraphs: Choose cells whose candidates fit a short list of slots, such as “5 in row 4.” Include any attached cells that depend on those slots. Make sure every candidate in the set uses at least one slot. Count each distinct house and digit once.
If the counts match, the cells need every slot. Remove an outside candidate that uses one, or an inside candidate that uses two.

copy.description: Count the main set and its attached cells together. Each highlighted cell needs a digit, and each listed house has room for that digit only once.

guide.start: Choose cells whose candidates fit a short list of slots, such as “5 in row 4.” Include any attached cells that depend on those slots.
guide.check: Make sure every candidate in the set uses at least one slot. Count each distinct house and digit once.
guide.reason: If the counts match, the cells need every slot. Remove an outside candidate that uses one, or an inside candidate that uses two.

lessons.title: Junior Exocet
lessons.summary: In a Junior Exocet, two target cells must contain the same two digits as a pair of base cells. The crossing lines leave too few other places for those digits. This can rule out target candidates before either base is solved.

blocks.title: Count the places on the three crossing lines

paragraphs: Choose two base cells on one line in one box. Find the targets in the other boxes of that band or stack. For each possible base digit, follow the three crossing lines. Outside the targets, count the houses that can still hold it.
Each crossing line needs a copy. If the other places can hold only two copies, a target must hold the third. Keep the choices that work for both base digits.

copy.description: Choose a possible digit in either base cell. Count its places on all three lines, first outside the targets and then inside them.

guide.start: Choose two base cells on one line in one box. Find the targets in the other boxes of that band or stack.
guide.check: For each possible base digit, follow the three crossing lines. Outside the targets, count the houses that can still hold it.
guide.reason: Each crossing line needs a copy. If the other places can hold only two copies, a target must hold the third. Keep the choices that work for both base digits.

lessons.title: Senior Exocet
lessons.summary: In a Senior Exocet, the digits in two base cells must also appear at the targets. One target can lie outside the band or stack that contains the bases. The crossing lines explain why each base digit needs a target.

blocks.title: Follow the crossing lines to the outer target
