paragraphs: Find two base cells in one box. Follow the crossing lines to the targets. One can lie beyond the band or stack that contains the bases. Count the places for each base digit across all three lines. If two cells act as one target, find the link that lets them do so.
Each crossing line needs the base digit. Too few places outside the targets force a copy into a target cell or group. Keep only assignments that supply both base digits.

copy.description: Trace a digit from the bases to its possible targets on all three lines. A grouped target can supply the digit in either of its linked cells.

guide.start: Find two base cells in one box. Follow the crossing lines to the targets. One can lie beyond the band or stack that contains the bases.
guide.check: Count the places for each base digit across all three lines. If two cells act as one target, find the link that lets them do so.
guide.reason: Each crossing line needs the base digit. Too few places outside the targets force a copy into a target cell or group. Keep only assignments that supply both base digits.

lessons.title: Double Exocet
lessons.summary: Two Exocets can each allow several choices on their own. When they share crossing lines, the choices must also fit together. A candidate with no compatible pair of arrangements is impossible.

blocks.title: Compare the choices for both base pairs

paragraphs: Find both base pairs and their targets. For each Exocet, list the choices that satisfy its three crossing lines. Pair a choice from the first Exocet with one from the second. Reject pairs that repeat a digit in a house or leave a crossing line short.
The puzzle must satisfy both patterns at once. Remove a candidate if it cannot occur with any compatible pair of choices.

copy.description: Try both target pairs together. A placement that fits one Exocet still needs room on the lines it shares with the other.

guide.start: Find both base pairs and their targets. For each Exocet, list the choices that satisfy its three crossing lines.
guide.check: Pair a choice from the first Exocet with one from the second. Reject pairs that repeat a digit in a house or leave a crossing line short.
guide.reason: The puzzle must satisfy both patterns at once. Remove a candidate if it cannot occur with any compatible pair of choices.

lessons.title: Franken Fish
lessons.summary: A Franken Fish uses a box among its base or cover houses. For one digit, the bases can use up all the space in the covers. Extra possibilities called fins can break that count.

blocks.title: Count a fish that includes a box

paragraphs: Pick one digit. Choose equally many base and cover houses, with a box on at least one side. Look for candidates outside the covers or in overlapping bases. These fins can change the count. Test the target against each one.
Without the fins, the bases use all the room in the covers. If placing the target also rules out every fin, it leaves too few places for the bases.

copy.description: Trace 9 through the marked lines and boxes. Include the possible 9 outside the usual cover count before removing a candidate.

guide.start: Pick one digit. Choose equally many base and cover houses, with a box on at least one side.
guide.check: Look for candidates outside the covers or in overlapping bases. These fins can change the count. Test the target against each one.
guide.reason: Without the fins, the bases use all the room in the covers. If placing the target also rules out every fin, it leaves too few places for the bases.

lessons.title: Mutant Fish
lessons.summary: In a Mutant Fish, rows and columns can appear together among the bases or the covers. The same cell can count toward more than one house. The removal follows only if the required copies cannot all fit with that candidate present.

blocks.title: Check the overlapping bases and covers

paragraphs: Choose one digit. Find base or cover houses that include both rows and columns. Boxes can also belong to the pattern. For each possible placement, count the bases it fills and covers it uses. Include uncovered places and places shared by multiple bases.
A placement that uses more covers than the bases can spare leaves too little room for the remaining base digits. A removal must also hold with every possible fin.

copy.description: Follow 4 through the marked houses. At each overlap, count each base and cover that the placement affects.

guide.start: Choose one digit. Find base or cover houses that include both rows and columns. Boxes can also belong to the pattern.
guide.check: For each possible placement, count the bases it fills and covers it uses. Include uncovered places and places shared by multiple bases.
guide.reason: A placement that uses more covers than the bases can spare leaves too little room for the remaining base digits. A removal must also hold with every possible fin.

lessons.title: Kraken Fish Type 1
lessons.summary: A fin is an extra possibility that can break an ordinary fish deduction. In a Type 1 Kraken Fish, the fish rules out a candidate when all fins are false. Each possible true fin rules it out by a chain.

blocks.title: Trace every fin to the fish’s removal

paragraphs: Find a finned fish. Set all its fins aside and identify a candidate the remaining fish rules out. Suppose a fin is true. Follow its chain to the same candidate. Repeat for every fin.
If all fins are false, the fish rules out the candidate. If a fin is true, its chain rules it out. Those cases cover every possibility.

copy.description: The target is a candidate 2. Check the fish with no fins and each chain that starts from a true fin.

guide.start: Find a finned fish. Set all its fins aside and identify a candidate the remaining fish rules out.
guide.check: Suppose a fin is true. Follow its chain to the same candidate. Repeat for every fin.
guide.reason: If all fins are false, the fish rules out the candidate. If a fin is true, its chain rules it out. Those cases cover every possibility.

references.label: HoDoKu on forcing proofs and Kraken Fish

lessons.title: Kraken Fish Type 2
lessons.summary: A Type 2 Kraken Fish follows the possible placements of a fish digit, including its fins. Together those cases cover every possible outcome. A candidate that fails in every case can even be a different digit.

blocks.title: Compare the chains from every possible placement

paragraphs: Choose a line or cover in the fish. List its possible required placements and all fins that can break the fish. Starting from each choice, trace the moves it forces. Look for a candidate that every branch rules out.
At least one listed choice must hold. If every choice rules out the same candidate, remove it. Its digit can differ from the fish digit.

copy.description: Follow each branch to the crossed-out 7. The branches can reach a cell outside the usual fish removals.

guide.start: Choose a line or cover in the fish. List its possible required placements and all fins that can break the fish.
guide.check: Starting from each choice, trace the moves it forces. Look for a candidate that every branch rules out.
guide.reason: At least one listed choice must hold. If every choice rules out the same candidate, remove it. Its digit can differ from the fish digit.

references.label: HoDoKu on forcing proofs and Kraken Fish

groups.title: Impossible
groups.overview: Compare nested cases or complete layouts for several digits.

lessons.title: Nested proofs and search
lessons.summary: A conclusion reached inside a trial depends on the assumption that led there. A nested proof tries another choice inside that trial. Its conclusion applies to the original grid only after the outer cases support it.

blocks.title: Keep the inner and outer choices separate

paragraphs: Suppose one starting choice is true. If the resulting grid still has two ways forward, test those choices separately within that case.

blocks.title: Keep each conclusion in its scope

paragraphs: Suppose the outer choice is A. Inside A, both possible values of B force C. You can now use C to continue the A case.
To use C on the original grid, every remaining outer case must also force C. Alternatively, a contradiction in A rules out A itself.

blocks.caption: What the search tells you
rows: The search reaches a time limit

blocks.title: Computer methods and human proofs

paragraphs: A solver can test a choice, follow its consequences, and return to the last choice if it fails. This is backtracking. Another approach compares complete layouts for one or more digits.
Impossible is the highest difficulty in the app. A player can still find a shorter proof than the solver found.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: Suppose A is true. Both possible cases for B force C. What do you know?
questions.explanation: C follows while A is true. The case where A is false is still open.

questions.prompt: A solver reaches its time limit. Does that prove the puzzle has no solution?
questions.explanation: An unexamined case can still contain a solution.

questions.prompt: Does finding a completed grid tell you the easiest move a player can use?
questions.explanation: A completion shows the final digits. Identifying an available technique requires a separate proof.

references.label: HoDoKu: templates, forcing nets, and brute force

lessons.title: Nested forcing net
lessons.summary: A nested forcing net compares several possibilities inside one branch of a larger proof. An inner contradiction rules out a choice in that branch. It rules out the outer assumption only if every way to continue the branch fails.

blocks.title: Branch where the outer trial still has a choice

paragraphs: Begin with an outer assumption. If direct moves stop, choose a cell or house with few choices inside that branch. Try all the inner choices separately. Carry a conclusion back to the outer branch only if every surviving inner choice supports it.
An inner proof tells you what follows from the outer assumption. To make a move on the original grid, finish the outer proof as well.

copy.description: Keep the outer assumption in view while you follow the inner branches. Compare their results before continuing the outer case.

guide.start: Begin with an outer assumption. If direct moves stop, choose a cell or house with few choices inside that branch.
guide.check: Try all the inner choices separately. Carry a conclusion back to the outer branch only if every surviving inner choice supports it.
guide.reason: An inner proof tells you what follows from the outer assumption. To make a move on the original grid, finish the outer proof as well.

lessons.title: Complete layouts for a digit
lessons.summary: A complete layout places one digit once in every row, column, and box, including its givens. A candidate needs at least one layout that uses its cell. Layouts for different digits must also fit together without sharing a cell.

blocks.title: Trace all nine copies of one digit

paragraphs: Choose one digit. Mark its givens and all its possible cells. Start in a row with very few choices.

blocks.title: A layout needs every house

paragraphs: A complete layout uses the digit once in every row, column, and box. It includes every copy already on the board. If no complete layout uses a candidate, remove it. If all layouts use it, place it.

blocks.title: Two digits cannot share a cell

paragraphs: Layouts for two different digits cannot share a cell. Discard a layout for 5 if every layout for 8 overlaps it.
For three digits, the three layouts must fit at the same time. Other digits can still rule out a combination that passes this test.

blocks.title: Check your understanding

questions.prompt: One layout omits a possible 5 and another uses it. Can you remove that 5 from this evidence?
questions.explanation: To remove it this way, every possible layout must omit it.

questions.prompt: A layout for 5 and a layout for 8 both use R3C8. Can those layouts occur together?
questions.explanation: R3C8 can hold only one of those digits. At least one layout must change.

lessons.title: Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Pattern Overlay compares all the ways one digit can fit across the grid. A cell that appears in every possible layout must hold the digit. A cell that appears in none cannot hold it.

blocks.title: List the possible layouts for one digit

paragraphs: Choose a digit. Include its placed copies and mark every remaining place it can go. Build layouts with one copy in each row, column, and box. Start in the row with the fewest choices.
If no complete layout uses a candidate, remove it. If every layout uses the same cell, place the digit there.

copy.description: Try 4 in R2C5. No arrangement that includes it can put one 4 in every row, column, and box.

guide.start: Choose a digit. Include its placed copies and mark every remaining place it can go.
guide.check: Build layouts with one copy in each row, column, and box. Start in the row with the fewest choices.
guide.reason: If no complete layout uses a candidate, remove it. If every layout uses the same cell, place the digit there.

lessons.title: Two-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Two different digits cannot share a cell. Two-digit Pattern Overlay keeps only pairs of complete layouts that fit side by side. A candidate disappears if no surviving pair uses it.

blocks.title: Find two layouts that fit together

paragraphs: Choose two digits. For each digit, list the ways it can appear once in every row, column, and box. Pair the layouts. Discard any pair that puts the two digits in the same cell.
A possible placement needs at least one pair of layouts that fit together. If no surviving pair uses the candidate, remove it.

copy.description: Compare the 3 layouts with the 7 layouts. Each crossed-out 7 forces an overlap with every possible layout for 3.

guide.start: Choose two digits. For each digit, list the ways it can appear once in every row, column, and box.
guide.check: Pair the layouts. Discard any pair that puts the two digits in the same cell.
guide.reason: A possible placement needs at least one pair of layouts that fit together. If no surviving pair uses the candidate, remove it.

lessons.title: Three-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: A layout for 4 can fit one for 5 and one for 6, yet have no way to fit both together. Three-digit Pattern Overlay requires all three layouts to fit at once. A candidate needs a place in at least one such combination.

blocks.title: Check three layouts on the same grid

paragraphs: Choose three digits with few possible layouts. Begin with layouts that each have a compatible partner for the other digits. Keep one layout for each digit. The three layouts must fit at the same time without sharing a cell.
A layout can fit each of two digits separately and still fail when both are present. Remove a candidate if no compatible triple uses it.

copy.description: Try 4 in R9C2. Every way to place the three digits with that 4 puts two of them in the same cell.

guide.start: Choose three digits with few possible layouts. Begin with layouts that each have a compatible partner for the other digits.
guide.check: Keep one layout for each digit. The three layouts must fit at the same time without sharing a cell.
guide.reason: A layout can fit each of two digits separately and still fail when both are present. Remove a candidate if no compatible triple uses it.

lessons.title: Four-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Four-digit Pattern Overlay fits four complete layouts onto one grid without sharing any cells. A placement common to every compatible group is forced. A candidate that appears in none is impossible.

blocks.title: Extend a compatible triple to four digits

paragraphs: Choose four digits whose possible layouts need some of the same cells. Start with compatible layouts for three of them. Try to add a fourth full layout without sharing a cell. Compare all the combinations that survive.
If every compatible combination puts a digit in one cell, place it there. If none uses a candidate, remove it.

copy.description: All four-digit combinations that fit the grid put 4 in R2C1.

guide.start: Choose four digits whose possible layouts need some of the same cells. Start with compatible layouts for three of them.
guide.check: Try to add a fourth full layout without sharing a cell. Compare all the combinations that survive.
guide.reason: If every compatible combination puts a digit in one cell, place it there. If none uses a candidate, remove it.

lessons.title: Five-digit Pattern Overlay
lessons.summary: Five-digit Pattern Overlay compares five complete layouts at once. A candidate can survive checks on smaller groups but leave nowhere to put the fifth digit. It must belong to a combination that fits all five.

blocks.title: Find a fifth layout that fits the other four

paragraphs: Choose five digits with few possible layouts. Begin with their compatible smaller groups. Add one complete layout per digit. Each new layout must avoid every cell the others already use.
A candidate needs a combination that fits all five digits at once. If none includes it, remove it even if it fits every smaller group.

copy.description: Try 9 in R2C5. No complete layout using that 9 leaves room for compatible layouts of all four other digits.

guide.start: Choose five digits with few possible layouts. Begin with their compatible smaller groups.
guide.check: Add one complete layout per digit. Each new layout must avoid every cell the others already use.
guide.reason: A candidate needs a combination that fits all five digits at once. If none includes it, remove it even if it fits every smaller group.

groups.title: X Sudoku
groups.overview: Each marked diagonal must also contain the digits 1 through 9.

lessons.title: Diagonal Locked Candidates
lessons.summary: A marked diagonal in X Sudoku needs each digit once. If all its possible 6s lie in one box, the diagonal must supply that box’s 6. The rest of the box cannot contain another one.

blocks.title: Check where a marked diagonal crosses a box

paragraphs: In X Sudoku, each marked diagonal needs the digits 1 through 9. Choose one digit and find all its possible places on that diagonal.
If those places lie in one box, the diagonal supplies the digit for that box. Remove it from cells in the box off the diagonal.

blocks.title: Start in a box

paragraphs: You can also start inside the box. If all its possible places for 3 lie on one marked diagonal, the box supplies that diagonal’s 3. Remove 3 from the rest of the diagonal.

blocks.instruction: Use the box and the marked diagonal to rule out one candidate.

guide.start: Choose a digit on the marked diagonal. Look for a box that contains several of its possible places.
guide.check: Read the whole box and the whole diagonal. Which one needs the digit in their shared cells?
guide.reason: One of the shared cells must hold the digit. That supplies both the box and the diagonal.

groups.title: Killer Sudoku
groups.overview: Use a cage total or the sum of a whole row, column, or box.

lessons.title: Killer cage combinations
lessons.summary: A Killer cage gives the sum of its digits, and its digits must all be different. A two-cell cage totaling 4 can only contain 1 and 3. Other cages can allow several combinations until nearby digits narrow them down.

blocks.title: Count the cells and read the cage total

paragraphs: Choose a small cage. Read its total and count its cells. List the ways that many different digits can add to the total. Then fit the digits of each combination into the individual cells.
A candidate needs a combination that actually puts it in that cell. If every such combination repeats a digit or needs an unavailable partner, remove it.

copy.description: R5C6 and R6C6 must add to 8. Their possible digit pairs are {1, 7}, {2, 6}, and {3, 5}. Two 4s would repeat a digit in the cage.

guide.start: Choose a small cage. Read its total and count its cells.
guide.check: List the ways that many different digits can add to the total. Then fit the digits of each combination into the individual cells.
guide.reason: A candidate needs a combination that actually puts it in that cell. If every such combination repeats a digit or needs an unavailable partner, remove it.

lessons.title: Killer cage and house sums
lessons.summary: Every complete row, column, or box adds up to 45. The totals of cages inside it can reveal the sum of the cells left over, even when those cells have no total of their own.

blocks.title: Find the cells left outside complete cages

paragraphs: Choose a row, column, or box that contains a whole cage. The nine digits in that house add to 45. Subtract the total of each full cage from 45. For a cage that crosses the boundary, count separately the cells inside and outside.
The uncovered cells must add to the remainder. For cells outside the house, subtract their inside partners’ sum from the total of the crossing cages.

copy.description: Box 4 totals 45. The three cage cells in its middle row total 12, so the six other cells must add to 33.

guide.start: Choose a row, column, or box that contains a whole cage. The nine digits in that house add to 45.
guide.check: Subtract the total of each full cage from 45. For a cage that crosses the boundary, count separately the cells inside and outside.
guide.reason: The uncovered cells must add to the remainder. For cells outside the house, subtract their inside partners’ sum from the total of the crossing cages.

groups.title: Chess variants
groups.overview: A knight’s move or a king’s move can rule out a matching digit.

lessons.title: Anti-Knight
lessons.summary: The Anti-Knight rule forbids two equal digits a chess knight’s move apart. A placed digit can therefore rule out a matching pencil mark across a box boundary, even when the cells share no house.

blocks.title: Trace a knight’s move from a known digit

paragraphs: From a cell, move two rows and one column, or two columns and one row. Look for another possible copy of the same digit. The two cells must hold different digits. Look for a placed digit or a cell with only one candidate left.
If one end must be 9, remove 9 from the other. The knight rule applies even when the cells share no row, column, or box.

copy.description: R1C3 and R2C5 are one row and two columns apart. Compare the possible 9s in these two cells.

guide.start: From a cell, move two rows and one column, or two columns and one row. Look for another possible copy of the same digit.
guide.check: The two cells must hold different digits. Look for a placed digit or a cell with only one candidate left.
guide.reason: If one end must be 9, remove 9 from the other. The knight rule applies even when the cells share no row, column, or box.

lessons.title: Anti-King
lessons.summary: Under the Anti-King rule, cells that touch at an edge or a corner must have different digits. The extra restriction matters at corners across box boundaries, where the usual row, column, and box rules allow a repeat.

blocks.title: Check diagonal neighbors across a box boundary

paragraphs: Start at a placed digit near a box corner. Check the cells one row and one column away.
Look for the same digit as a candidate in those cells, especially across a box or region border. Cells in the same row, column, or box already have to differ.

copy.description: R2C3 is 8. R1C4 touches it diagonally, so remove 8 from R1C4.

guide.start: Start at a placed digit near a box corner. Check the cells one row and one column away.
guide.check: Look for the same digit as a candidate in those cells, especially across a box or region border. Cells in the same row, column, or box already have to differ.
guide.reason: The two cells are one king’s move apart, so they must differ. The placed digit rules out its matching candidate.

references.label: King of Diamonds by Philip Newman

groups.title: Thermometer
groups.overview: The digits increase from the bulb toward the tip.

lessons.title: Thermometers
lessons.summary: Digits on a thermometer rise from its bulb to its tip. Every cell needs room for the smaller digits before it and the larger digits after it. A long thermometer can narrow a cell even on an otherwise empty grid.

blocks.title: Count the cells before and after a position

paragraphs: Count the cells before and after the position you want to fill. The third cell from the bulb must be at least 3. A cell with two more cells after it can be at most 7.
A thermometer can skip numbers. Check that a sequence of larger digits still fits all the way to the tip. A given or a short candidate list can narrow the range further.

copy.description: The path runs from R4C7 through R4C6 to R3C6. Two smaller digits must come before the tip, so R3C6 cannot be 1.

guide.start: Read from the round bulb to the tip. Each digit must be larger than the previous digit. A step can skip a number.
guide.check: Count the cells before and after the cell you want to fill. For example, the third cell from the bulb must be at least 3.
guide.reason: A candidate must fit an increasing sequence across the whole thermometer. A given or a short candidate list can narrow the range further.

groups.title: Arrow
groups.overview: The digits along the arrow add to the digit in its circle.

lessons.title: Arrows
lessons.summary: The digit in an arrow’s circle equals the sum of the digits along its shaft. A small circle digit limits how large any one shaft digit can be. Known shaft digits narrow the circle in return.

blocks.title: Compare the circle with the sum on its arrow

paragraphs: Find the circle and follow its arrow. Count the cells on the arrow after the circle. Try a possible total in the circle. Find a digit for each arrow cell so their sum equals that total.
Every part of the sum must fit its own cell. Digits on the arrow can repeat only where the other puzzle rules permit it.

copy.description: R1C6 is the circle. The arrow passes through R2C7 and ends on 1 in R1C8. The circle must be one more than R2C7.

guide.start: Find the circle and follow its arrow. Count the cells on the arrow after the circle.
guide.check: Try a possible total in the circle. Find a digit for each arrow cell so their sum equals that total.
guide.reason: Every part of the sum must fit its own cell. Digits on the arrow can repeat only where the other puzzle rules permit it.

groups.title: Kropki
groups.overview: Dots tell you how two neighboring digits are related.

lessons.title: Kropki dots
lessons.summary: A Kropki dot gives a relationship between two neighboring digits. A white dot means they differ by one. A black dot means one is twice the other. A candidate needs a partner that fits the dot.

blocks.title: Check the possible partners across a dot

paragraphs: Pick a candidate on one side of a dot and find its possible partners across the dot. A 3 beside a white dot needs 2 or 4. Beside a black dot it needs 6. Only 1 and 2 satisfy both dot rules as a pair.
Remove a candidate if no partner fits the marked rule. An unmarked edge excludes a relation only when the puzzle says that all dots of that kind are given.

copy.description: The white dot joins R7C7 to a 2 in R7C8. Only 1 or 3 can sit across a white dot from 2.

guide.start: For a white dot, the two digits differ by one. For a black dot, one digit is twice the other.
guide.check: Pick a candidate on one side and find its possible partners across the dot. If both kinds of dot apply, only 1 and 2 fit.
guide.reason: Remove a candidate if no partner fits the marked rule. An unmarked edge excludes a relation only when the puzzle says that all dots of that kind are given.

groups.title: Other cell and pair rules
groups.overview: Find which digits can fill marked cells or neighboring pairs.

lessons.title: Odd and even cells
lessons.summary: A parity clue tells you whether a marked cell contains an odd or even digit. For example, an even cell can hold only 2, 4, 6, or 8 before you consider the rest of its row, column, and box.

blocks.title: Read the odd or even mark

paragraphs: A circle marks an odd cell. A square marks an even cell. Unmarked cells can contain either.
Compare the candidates with the allowed digits. Odd cells allow 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9. Even cells allow 2, 4, 6, or 8.

copy.description: Find the marked cell. Its circle or square tells you which digits to keep.
copy.reason: A digit of the other parity cannot satisfy the clue. Remove it even if the ordinary row, column, and box still allow it.

guide.start: Find an odd circle or an even square.
guide.check: Compare the candidates with the allowed digits. Odd cells allow 1, 3, 5, 7, or 9. Even cells allow 2, 4, 6, or 8.
guide.reason: A digit of the other parity cannot satisfy the clue. Remove it even if the ordinary row, column, and box still allow it.

lessons.title: Non-consecutive neighbors
lessons.summary: In a non-consecutive puzzle, cells that share an edge cannot hold consecutive digits. A placed 5 therefore rules out 4 and 6 in its edge neighbors, in addition to the usual Sudoku restrictions.

blocks.title: Check the cells that share an edge

paragraphs: Start with a placed digit. Check its neighbors above, below, left, and right.
Look for candidates one less or one more than that digit. For 1, check only 2. For 9, check only 8.
Some mixed puzzles exempt the pairs marked by white dots. Check the puzzle’s rule description before using Non-Consecutive across a dot.

copy.description: R1C4 is 5. R2C4 shares its lower edge, so R2C4 cannot be 6.

guide.start: Choose a placed digit and look directly above, below, left, and right of it.
guide.check: A neighbor across an edge cannot differ by one. Next to 5, for example, neither 4 nor 6 fits.
guide.reason: Near 1, the consecutive digit to remove is 2. Near 9, it is 8. Diagonal neighbors do not share an edge.

references.label: Literally No One by Philip Newman

lessons.title: Non-Consecutive locked candidates (2 cells)
lessons.summary: Two adjacent locations for a digit rule out the digit one less or one more in those cells. Either candidate would leave their house with no place for its required digit.

blocks.title: Find two adjacent locations for one digit

paragraphs: Find a row, column, box, or variant house where a digit has exactly two possible locations. The two cells must share an edge, and Non-Consecutive must apply across that edge.
A candidate one less or one more cannot go in either cell. It would exclude the required digit from its own cell and from the other cell. The house would have nowhere for that digit.

copy.description: In row 1, 7 can go only in R1C7 or R1C8.
copy.reason: Remove 6 from R1C7. If R1C7 were 6, it could not be 7, and Non-Consecutive would forbid 7 in the adjacent R1C8. Row 1 would have no 7.

guide.start: Find a digit with exactly two locations in one house.
guide.check: Check that the locations share an edge and that no exception exempts it.
guide.follow: Look for candidates one less or one more in either location.
guide.reason: Either candidate would exclude the required digit from both locations.

lessons.title: Non-Consecutive locked candidates (3 cells)
lessons.summary: A digit confined around one target can rule out a neighboring digit there. Every location for the required digit must be that target or its active Non-Consecutive neighbor.

blocks.title: Check every location around one target

paragraphs: Find a house whose possible locations for a digit fit into three cells around a target. Every location must be the target itself or share an active Non-Consecutive edge with it.

Remove a candidate one less or one more from the target. It would exclude the required digit from every possible location. The target need not be a location for the required digit: two locations on opposite sides can give the same deduction.
Check the entire house for another location. A location beyond these cells breaks the argument.

copy.description: In row 6, 4 can go only in R6C4, R6C5, or R6C6.
copy.reason: Remove 5 from R6C5. It would exclude 4 from R6C5 itself and from both adjacent locations, leaving no 4 in row 6.

guide.start: Find a digit confined to two or three locations in one house.
guide.check: Choose a target that is one of those locations or shares an active Non-Consecutive edge with each of them. The complete pattern must span three cells.
guide.follow: Check the target for candidates one less or one more.
guide.reason: The candidate would leave the house with no location for its required digit.

lessons.title: Non-Consecutive bivalue
lessons.summary: A cell with only two consecutive candidates rules out both digits in its edge neighbors. One choice would repeat a digit in their shared house; the other would violate Non-Consecutive.

blocks.title: Find two consecutive candidates in one cell

paragraphs: Find an empty cell with exactly two candidates that differ by 1, such as 3 and 4. Check each cell that shares an active Non-Consecutive edge with it.
Neither 3 nor 4 can go in such a neighbor. One choice would repeat a digit in their shared row or column. The other would put consecutive digits across the edge.
Check for edge exceptions first. The digits 1 and 9 do not count as consecutive.

copy.description: R4C4 can contain only 3 or 4.
copy.reason: Remove 3 from R4C3. If R4C3 were 3, a 3 in R4C4 would repeat it in row 4, while a 4 there would violate Non-Consecutive.

guide.start: Find a cell with exactly two consecutive candidates.
guide.check: Choose a neighbor across an edge where Non-Consecutive applies.
guide.follow: Check whether either of the two digits remains in that neighbor.
guide.reason: Both choices for the source cell would conflict: one repeats a digit in a shared house, and the other differs by 1.

lessons.title: Non-Consecutive trivalue
lessons.summary: A cell restricted to three consecutive digits rules out their middle digit in its edge neighbors. A neighboring middle digit would leave the source cell with no candidate.

blocks.title: Look for three consecutive candidates

paragraphs: Find a cell restricted to three consecutive candidates, such as 5, 6, and 7. Check the cells across its active Non-Consecutive edges.
A 6 in a neighbor would rule out 5 and 7 through Non-Consecutive. It would also rule out 6 in the source cell through their shared row or column. Remove 6 from the neighbor.
The same argument works when only the two outer candidates remain. Check the full candidate list: another candidate outside that range would break the argument.

copy.description: R4C4 can contain only 5, 6, or 7.
copy.reason: Remove 6 from R3C4. Non-Consecutive would rule out 5 and 7 in R4C4, while column 4 would rule out a second 6.

guide.start: Find a cell whose candidates fit within three consecutive digits.
guide.check: Both outer digits must remain; the middle digit can be present or already removed.
guide.follow: Look for the middle digit in a neighbor across an active Non-Consecutive edge.
guide.reason: The neighbor's middle digit conflicts with every candidate in the source cell.

lessons.title: Inequality
lessons.summary: An inequality sign puts two cells in order. Every possible digit on the smaller side needs a larger partner on the other side. The largest and smallest available partners set the limits for both cells.

blocks.title: Compare the limits on either side of the sign

paragraphs: Read A < B as “A is smaller than B.” The narrow end of the sign points toward the smaller digit. Try the largest candidate in B. Any candidate in A that is at least that large has no possible partner.
Use the smallest candidate in A to check B the same way. Each candidate needs at least one partner on the correct side of the inequality.

copy.description: The clue says R5C9 < R6C9. R6C9 cannot be 1 because R5C9 needs a smaller digit.

guide.start: Read A < B as “A is smaller than B.” The narrow end of the sign points toward the smaller digit.
guide.check: Try the largest candidate in B. Any candidate in A that is at least that large has no possible partner.
guide.reason: Use the smallest candidate in A to check B the same way. Each candidate needs at least one partner on the correct side of the inequality.

lessons.title: Clone cells
lessons.summary: Cells with the same Clone letter contain the same digit. Compare their candidates: a digit ruled out in one copy cannot go in any matching copy. Different letters can still use the same digit if their other rules allow it.

blocks.title: Compare matching positions in the copies

paragraphs: Find cells marked with the same Clone letter. Compare their candidate lists. If one copy already contains 7, every matching copy must be 7. Otherwise, find the digits that appear in every list.
All matching cells need the same digit. If any one copy rules out a digit, remove it from the other copies too.

copy.description: R9C4 and R2C3 both carry Clone A, so their digits must match. A candidate that appears in only one of those cells cannot fill either.

guide.start: Find cells marked with the same Clone letter. Compare their candidate lists.
guide.check: If one copy already contains 7, every matching copy must be 7. Otherwise, find the digits that appear in every list.
guide.reason: All matching cells need the same digit. If any one copy rules out a digit, remove it from the other copies too.

references.label: Bill Murphy: Legs in a Snare

lessons.title: XV sums
lessons.summary: An XV clue gives the sum of two neighboring cells. V means 5 and X means 10. Each choice in one cell fixes the digit required in the other.

blocks.title: Find the missing partner for a marked sum

paragraphs: Find a marked pair. Choose the cell with fewer candidates and read the total on the mark. Subtract a candidate from the total. The remainder is the digit required in the other cell.
If that partner cannot go in the other cell, remove the candidate. Use unmarked edges only if the puzzle says all marks of that kind are given.

copy.description: The V between R7C1 and R8C1 means their digits add to 5. A 9 already exceeds the total.

guide.start: Find a marked pair. Choose the cell with fewer candidates and read the total on the mark.
guide.check: Subtract a candidate from the total. The remainder is the digit required in the other cell.
guide.reason: If that partner cannot go in the other cell, remove the candidate. Use unmarked edges only if the puzzle says all marks of that kind are given.

lessons.title: Two-cell sums
lessons.summary: A Roman numeral gives the total of two neighboring cells. XV means 15. Subtract one candidate from the total to find its required partner.

blocks.title: Match each candidate to its required partner

paragraphs: Start with a marked pair that has few candidates. Subtract each candidate from the total. The result must be a digit that can go in the other cell.
If the required partner is outside 1–9 or cannot go in that cell, remove the candidate. The cells share a row or column, so they cannot both contain the same digit.

copy.description: The XV between R7C1 and R8C1 means a total of 15. R7C1 must be 8, so R8C1 needs 7. Remove 1 from R8C1.

guide.start: Find the total between the two cells. Start with the cell that has fewer candidates.
guide.check: Subtract a candidate from the total. Find the required partner in the other cell.
guide.reason: Remove the candidate if its partner cannot go in the other cell. A repeated digit is also forbidden by their shared row or column.

groups.title: Other line rules
groups.overview: Compare digits along a line using its order, range, or sum.

lessons.title: Palindrome lines
lessons.summary: A palindrome line reads the same in both directions. Its two ends match, as do the cells one step in from each end. A known digit or a missing candidate in one cell affects its partner.

blocks.title: Compare the cells at matching distances from the ends

paragraphs: Find the first and last cells on the palindrome. The sequence must read the same in both directions. Match the two ends, then move one cell inward on each side. An odd-length line has an unpaired middle cell. The Palindrome rule places no extra restriction on that cell.
For each matched pair, keep the digits that appear in both cells. If one end already has a digit, the other end needs that digit too.

copy.description: R6C9 and R7C7 are the ends of a three-cell palindrome. R6C9 is 9, so R7C7 must also be 9.

guide.start: Find the first and last cells on the palindrome. The sequence must read the same in both directions.
guide.check: Match the two ends, then move one cell inward on each side. An odd-length line has an unpaired middle cell. The Palindrome rule places no extra restriction on that cell.
guide.reason: For each matched pair, keep the digits that appear in both cells. If one end already has a digit, the other end needs that digit too.

lessons.title: Between lines
lessons.summary: The two ends of a Between line set a range. Every digit inside the line must lie strictly between them. The interior digits can appear in any order.

blocks.title: Compare the two end digits

paragraphs: Try a digit in each endpoint circle. If the ends are 2 and 6, every interior cell needs a 3, 4, or 5. Reject those ends if an interior cell has none of those candidates.
Compare the endpoint pairs that remain. Remove an interior candidate if none of those pairs leaves room for it.

copy.description: The circles contain 8 in R6C8 and 4 in R5C8, so interior digits must be 5, 6, or 7. Remove 9 from R5C7.

guide.start: Read the two circles at the ends. Every digit between them must be larger than the smaller end and smaller than the larger end.
guide.check: Try an endpoint pair. Find at least one digit in that range for every interior cell. The interior digits can appear in any order.
guide.reason: Reject a pair if any interior cell cannot fit. Remove an interior candidate if no possible pair leaves room for it.

lessons.title: Whispers lines
lessons.summary: A Whispers line requires a minimum difference between neighboring digits. On a German Whispers line with a gap of at least 5, low and high digits alternate. No digit is far enough from 5 to be its neighbor.

blocks.title: Compare the candidates in neighboring line cells

paragraphs: Read the minimum difference in the clue. Compare a candidate in one cell with the digits in the next cell. With a minimum of 5, a 2 can sit beside only 7, 8, or 9.
An interior cell needs a partner on both sides. If no digit in either neighboring cell is far enough away, remove the candidate.

copy.description: This line needs a difference of at least 5. Compare each end with the middle cell, R3C3.

guide.start: Read the minimum difference for the line. German Whispers usually requires at least 5 between neighbors.
guide.check: For each candidate, compare the digits in the next cell. With a minimum of 5, a 2 can sit beside only 7, 8, or 9.
guide.reason: An interior cell needs a partner on both sides. If no digit in either neighboring cell is far enough away, remove the candidate.

lessons.title: Whispers and shared houses
lessons.summary: Line cells that share a row, column, box, or region must contain different digits. Use this restriction together with the line’s minimum difference to rule out candidates that the line alone still allows.

blocks.title: Find line cells that share a house

paragraphs: Start with a bend whose two ends are in one house. The ends need different digits even when they are separated along the line.

In this example, the two ends can contain only 3 and 4. If the middle cell were 8, both ends would need 3 to meet the minimum difference of 5. The shared box rules out that repeat, so remove 8 from the middle cell.
For a longer line, keep only the complete digit sequences that satisfy every link and each shared house. A digit with no surviving sequence can be removed.

copy.description: R2C4 and R2C5 each allow 3 or 4. If R1C5 were 8, both ends would need 3, repeating it in box 2. Remove 8 from R1C5.

guide.start: Find line cells that share a house. Read the minimum difference for the line.
guide.check: Try a candidate in the middle cell. Check whether the neighboring cells would have to repeat a digit in their shared house.
guide.reason: Every candidate needs a complete line assignment that also respects the shared houses. Remove it if no assignment fits.

lessons.title: Global Entropy
lessons.summary: Every 2 × 2 area needs a low digit (1–3), a medium digit (4–6) and a high digit (7–9). If only one cell can provide a missing group, remove its candidates from the other groups. One of the three groups appears twice.

blocks.title: Find a group that has only one place

paragraphs: Inspect four cells that form a 2 × 2 area. Include areas that cross box or region borders. Identify the groups of placed digits and cells whose candidates all belong to one group.
Each group needs its own cell. If two groups are confined to the same two cells, those cells must provide one from each group. Remove candidates from the third group in those cells.
A repeated group is required because four cells use three groups. Equal digits can repeat diagonally across box boundaries if all other puzzle rules allow it.

copy.description: R1C8 is 9 and R2C9 is 7, both high digits. R1C9 can only be 6, a medium digit. The area needs a low digit in R2C8. Remove 4 and 6, leaving 3.

guide.start: Inspect each digit group in the highlighted 2 × 2 area.
guide.check: Find a group with one possible cell, or two groups confined to two cells.
guide.reason: Every group needs a separate cell, so those cells cannot use candidates from another group.

references.label: Published Ordered Entropy puzzle by Philip Newman

lessons.title: Quadruples and Global Entropy
lessons.summary: A Quadruple circle fixes which digits must fit in a 2 × 2 area. When the puzzle uses Global Entropy, fit those digits and leave room for a low, medium, and high digit.

blocks.title: Fit the printed digits and all three groups

paragraphs: Start with a circle that prints two digits from one group. Those digits use two of the four cells, so the other cells must supply one digit from each missing group. A digit printed twice needs two cells.

If the circle area still has several possible arrangements, check the 2 × 2 area on the other side of an edge. The two shared cells must use the same digits in both areas. Keep an arrangement only if both areas have all three groups and the digits respect their shared rows, columns, and boxes or regions.

copy.description: R2C8 is 6 and the circle also needs 5. Only R2C9 can supply 5. R3C9 is 1, so R3C8 must supply the high digit. Remove 3 from R3C8.

drills.title: Fit the circle and its neighbors

guide.start: Read the digits in the circle and find the groups they already supply.
guide.check: Try a candidate. Fit the remaining printed digits and leave room for every missing group. If two areas share an edge, check the same digits in their shared cells.
guide.reason: Remove a candidate when every arrangement that uses it breaks a circle, an entropy area, or a shared house.

lessons.title: Modular lines
lessons.summary: A Modular line repeats three groups: {1, 4, 7}, {2, 5, 8} and {3, 6, 9}. Every three successive positions use one digit from each group. Positions three steps apart share a group, but can contain different digits.

blocks.title: Follow the three repeating groups

paragraphs: Look for a placed digit or a cell whose candidates all belong to one group. Follow that group every three positions along its own path. The other two positions must use the other two groups.
Two-cell lines use different groups. A one-cell path has no extra restriction. Touching paths remain independent. A closed line must fit the repeating pattern at its join.

copy.description: R5C6 is 3, in the group {3, 6, 9}. R4C7 must use a different group, so remove 6 from R4C7.

guide.start: Identify which groups remain possible in each highlighted cell.
guide.check: Follow the repeating groups along this path. Two-cell lines need different groups.
guide.reason: Remove a candidate if no allowed group order can use it.

references.label: Birbs of Paradise by Philip Newman

lessons.title: Entropic lines
lessons.summary: An Entropic line repeats three digit groups: low (1–3), medium (4–6) and high (7–9). Once you know two groups, the next position needs the third. Positions three steps apart share a group, but can contain different digits.

blocks.title: Find a cell confined to one digit group

paragraphs: Look for a placed digit or a cell whose candidates all belong to one group. Along the line, every three successive positions must use the three different groups. Follow that pattern in both directions.
Two-cell lines also use different groups. Touching paths remain independent. A closed line must fit the repeating pattern at its join.

copy.description: R5C6 can only be 3, a low digit. The two-cell line requires a different group in R6C6, so remove its low candidates.

guide.start: Identify low, medium and high candidates on the highlighted path.
guide.check: Follow the repeating groups. Two-cell lines need two different groups.
guide.reason: A candidate must fit a group order allowed by every cell on its own path.

references.label: Published Numeric Keypad puzzle by Clover

lessons.title: Group order contradiction
lessons.summary: Try an order for the groups on an Entropic or Modular line. Follow its effect on nearby clues until a rule makes that order impossible.

blocks.title: Look for a pair clue near the line

paragraphs: Pick one possible order for the first three groups. Apply that order to the line and keep track of which candidates remain.
Check a dot, sum mark, or inequality near the line. Use those restrictions in the houses or other repeating lines they touch.
One rule can make the order fail. For example, a white dot needs consecutive digits. If no pair of candidates differs by one across the dot, rule out the order you tried.
Remove a candidate if its group is missing from that position in every remaining order.

guide.start: Choose an order for the first three groups.
guide.check: Use each nearby clue to narrow candidates, one rule at a time.
guide.reason: A group order fails if it leaves a clue, house, or line with no valid assignment.

lessons.title: Repeating groups and houses
lessons.summary: Check which repeating groups on an Entropic or Modular line fit the candidates in a shared house. Each digit in the house needs its own cell.

blocks.title: Find a house crossed by the line

paragraphs: Mark the first three positions on the line. Every third cell uses the same group. On an Entropic line, the groups are 1–3, 4–6, and 7–9. On a Modular line, they are 1, 4, 7, then 2, 5, 8, and 3, 6, 9.
Try an order for the three groups that fits the candidates along the line. Check the row, column, or region it crosses. If two required digits have only one cell between them, that order fails.
Look at the assignments that still fit the house and line. If none use a candidate in its own cell, remove that candidate.

guide.start: Look for several cells from one line that share a house.
guide.check: Try the group orders that fit the line. Count where the house can place each digit.
guide.reason: An order fails if the house has too few places for the digits that it needs.

lessons.title: Renban lines
lessons.summary: A Renban line contains different consecutive digits in any order. A four-cell line that contains both 3 and 6 must also contain 4 and 5, even before you know their positions.

blocks.title: Find consecutive ranges of the right length

paragraphs: Count the cells on the line. A three-cell Renban needs three different consecutive digits, such as {3, 4, 5}. Find ranges of that length that include all the placed digits. Try a different digit from the range in each cell.
A candidate must fit a complete range and have a place in its own cell. The digits can appear in any order along the line.

copy.description: The line has three cells and already contains 4 and 5. Only {3, 4, 5} or {4, 5, 6} can fit, so the last cell cannot be 8.

guide.start: Count the cells on the line. A three-cell Renban needs three different consecutive digits, such as {3, 4, 5}.
guide.check: Find ranges of that length that include all the placed digits. Try a different digit from the range in each cell.
guide.reason: A candidate must fit a complete range and have a place in its own cell. The digits can appear in any order along the line.

lessons.title: Renban locked digit
lessons.summary: Every possible set for a Renban can share a digit. If its possible positions for that digit all lie in one row, column, or region, remove the digit from the rest of that house.

blocks.title: Find a digit in every possible set

paragraphs: List the consecutive sets that fit the line and its candidates. A digit that appears in every set must go somewhere on the line. For instance, every set of five consecutive Sudoku digits includes 5.
Find every position where the required digit can go on the line. If those positions all share a house, the digit must be in one of them. Cross it out from the remaining cells in that house.

copy.description: The four-cell Renban in row 6 can use 4–7, 5–8, or 6–9. Every set contains 6, so the line must supply the 6 for row 6.

guide.start: Find a digit that appears in every set that fits the Renban.
guide.check: Check where that digit can go on the line. Look for a house shared by all those positions.
guide.reason: One of those positions must supply that house’s copy of the digit. Remove the digit from the other cells in the house.

lessons.title: Renban in one house
lessons.summary: When an entire Renban lies in one house, its consecutive set leaves a specific set of digits for the rest of that house. Check both parts before choosing a set.

blocks.title: Check the cells off the line

paragraphs: List the consecutive sets that fit the line. For each set, cross its digits off your list of digits for the other cells in the house. Check whether those other cells can each use a different remaining digit.

Look for a cell off the line with just two candidates. If both of its digits were used off the line, any consecutive set that needs one of them would fail. When every set needs at least one, a second cell off the line cannot force the pair to use both digits.

guide.start: Find a Renban entirely inside one row, column, or region.
guide.check: For each set that fits the line, try assigning the remaining digits to the other cells in the house.
guide.reason: A candidate must fit a complete assignment of the house using one consecutive set on the line.

lessons.title: Renban and group counts
lessons.summary: Use the possible Renban sets to count how many cells in a house need digits from 1–4 or 6–9. A house can use each of those four digits once.

blocks.title: Look for Renbans that need the same four digits

paragraphs: A four-cell Renban without a place for 5 must use either 1–4 or 6–9. A three-cell Renban needs three consecutive digits. When its candidates rule out every set on one side of 5, look at where its remaining digits go.
Try a candidate that affects several Renbans. Check which sets can still fit each line. If that choice forces five cells in a house into the same group of four digits, remove the candidate you tried.
Sometimes the count first rules out a Renban set. If the remaining sets force a digit into one cell, check what that placement does to nearby lines and houses.

guide.start: Find several Renbans that share cells with one house.
guide.check: Try a candidate that limits the consecutive sets on those lines. Count how many cells in the house must use 1–4 or 6–9.
guide.reason: Five cells in one house cannot use just four distinct digits.

lessons.title: Region Sum lines
lessons.summary: A Region Sum line has the same total in each part defined by the region boundaries and the puzzle’s rules. A part with just one cell can set the total for all the others.

blocks.title: Compare the totals of the line’s parts

paragraphs: Trace the line across the region boundaries. Each part must have the same sum. If the clue groups repeat visits to a region, combine those visits. Start with the shortest part. Write down the totals its cells can make. Compare those totals with what the other parts can make.
A one-cell part sets the sum directly once you know its digit. Remove a candidate if its part cannot reach any shared total with it.

copy.description: R7C6 is alone in its part and contains 7. The other part, R7C7 and R8C7, must also add to 7.

guide.start: Trace the line across the region boundaries. Each part must have the same sum. If the clue groups repeat visits to a region, combine those visits.
guide.check: Start with the shortest part. Write down the totals its cells can make. Compare those totals with what the other parts can make.
guide.reason: A one-cell part sets the sum directly once you know its digit. Remove a candidate if its part cannot reach any shared total with it.

groups.title: Outside clues
groups.overview: Follow the cells named by the clue at the edge of the grid.

lessons.title: Little Killer sums
lessons.summary: A Little Killer clue gives the sum of all cells on a diagonal ray. Placed digits reduce the total left for its empty cells. The usual house rules determine where a digit can repeat along the ray.

blocks.title: Trace the diagonal named by the clue

paragraphs: Follow the arrow from the clue and count only the cells on its ray. Subtract the placed digits from the total. Compare the remainder with the smallest and largest sums the empty cells can reach. Then try the candidates that fit those bounds.
Each digit needs a way to complete the sum. A digit can repeat along the ray if the other puzzle rules allow the two cells to match.

copy.description: The ray totals 41. Its placed digits are 2, 6, and 9, so the four empty cells must add to 24.

guide.start: Follow the arrow from the clue and count only the cells on its ray. Subtract the placed digits from the total.
guide.check: Compare the remainder with the smallest and largest sums the empty cells can reach. Then try the candidates that fit those bounds.
guide.reason: Each digit needs a way to complete the sum. A digit can repeat along the ray if the other puzzle rules allow the two cells to match.

lessons.title: Little Killer and shared houses
lessons.summary: Digits on a Little Killer diagonal may repeat where the cells share no house. Check where the diagonal enters the same box, region, or extra house more than once to narrow the possible sums.

blocks.title: Check the total and shared houses

paragraphs: Group the diagonal cells that share a house. Their digits must differ within that group.
List the subtotals each group can make with distinct digits. Combine them to reach the printed sum.
Remove a candidate if no assignment reaches the total while keeping the digits distinct in each shared house.

guide.start: Group the diagonal cells that share a house. Their digits must differ within that group.
guide.check: List the subtotals each group can make with distinct digits. Combine them to reach the printed sum.
guide.reason: Remove a candidate if no assignment reaches the total while keeping the digits distinct in each shared house.

lessons.title: Renban sum and shared houses
lessons.summary: When a Little Killer diagonal contains a Renban, every valid set on the line leaves a fixed sum for the other cells. A shared house can rule out combinations that fit both printed clues.

blocks.title: Check the total and shared houses

paragraphs: Find a Little Killer diagonal with a Renban entirely on it. Identify the diagonal cells that share houses.
Try each consecutive set on the Renban. Subtract its sum from the printed total, then check the remaining cells for repeats in their houses.
Remove a candidate when every assignment that reaches the total and fits the Renban repeats a digit in a shared house.

guide.start: Find a Little Killer diagonal with a Renban entirely on it. Identify the diagonal cells that share houses.
guide.check: Try each consecutive set on the Renban. Subtract its sum from the printed total, then check the remaining cells for repeats in their houses.
guide.reason: Remove a candidate when every assignment that reaches the total and fits the Renban repeats a digit in a shared house.

lessons.title: Renban and Little Killer
lessons.summary: When a Little Killer diagonal contains a whole Renban, each possible set of consecutive digits leaves a different total for the other cells on the diagonal. Compare those totals to rule out candidates.

blocks.title: Subtract the sum of each Renban set

paragraphs: Look for a Renban with all of its cells on the same Little Killer diagonal. List the sets of consecutive digits that can fit the Renban candidates. Each set has the same sum in any order.
Subtract each set’s sum from the Little Killer total. Check whether the other cells on the diagonal can make the remainder. Cross out any candidate that cannot fit a set and a remainder together.

copy.description: The diagonal totals 19. Only the set {2, 3, 4} fits the Renban and leaves a sum the other two cells can make. The set adds to 9. R8C4 is already 3, so R9C5 must be 7.

guide.start: Find the Renban whose cells all lie on the Little Killer diagonal.
guide.check: For each consecutive set that fits the Renban, subtract its sum from the total. See whether the remaining cells can make that remainder.
guide.reason: A candidate must appear in an assignment that fits both the Renban and the Little Killer total.

lessons.title: Renban and Little Killer with a shared house
lessons.summary: A second Renban can limit a Little Killer diagonal through a shared house. The digits on that Renban are unavailable in the other cells of the house. Use those exclusions to check which candidates fit the diagonal and its total.

blocks.title: Match the shared cell and rule out repeats

paragraphs: Look for a Little Killer diagonal with a Renban entirely on it. Then find a second Renban that meets the diagonal in just one cell. Look for a house containing the second Renban and one more cell from the diagonal.

List the consecutive sets that fit the second Renban. For each set, keep the digits that can go in its shared cell. Cross the set’s digits out of the other diagonal cell in the house. Test the new candidates against the first Renban and the printed total.
Remove a candidate if it fails in every case. The rest of the diagonal only follows the usual rule about repeats in any houses its cells share.

copy.description: The 19 diagonal starts at R9C5. Its first two cells share box 8 with the Renban across R9C4, R9C5, and R9C6. Test each set on that Renban and exclude its digits from R8C4.

drills.title: Renban and Little Killer with a shared house

guide.start: Find the second Renban and the house it shares with the two cells of the diagonal.
guide.check: Try a consecutive set on that Renban. Keep its possible digits at the intersection, and exclude all its digits from the other diagonal cell in the house.
guide.reason: Keep candidates that fit the printed total and the contained Renban in at least one case.

lessons.title: Skyscrapers clues
lessons.summary: In a Skyscrapers clue, each digit is the height of a building. A taller building hides every shorter building behind it until the view reaches an even taller one. The outside clue counts the buildings you can see from that side.

blocks.title: Count visible buildings from the clue side

paragraphs: Read the cells from the edge nearest the clue. Count the first building, then count a building only when it exceeds the tallest one so far. A 9 hides every later building. A clue of 1 puts the 9 first.
Try a candidate and count how many buildings the remaining cells can reveal. Remove it if no order reaches the clue count.

copy.description: Look across row 9 from the left. The clue is 4, and the 9 in R9C7 hides both buildings after it.

guide.start: Read the cells from the edge nearest the clue. Each digit is a building height. Count the first building.
guide.check: Count another building only if it is taller than every one before it. A 9 hides all later buildings. A clue of 1 puts the 9 first.
guide.reason: Try a candidate and count how many buildings the remaining cells can reveal. Remove it if no order reaches the clue count.

lessons.title: Sandwich sums
lessons.summary: A Sandwich clue gives the sum of the digits strictly between 1 and 9 in a row or column. The endpoints can appear in either order. Their positions decide how many cells contribute to the sum.

blocks.title: Find the possible positions of 1 and 9

paragraphs: Find the possible places for 1 and 9. Either can be closer to the clue. Leave both out of the sum. For each pair of endpoints, add the digits strictly between them. A zero clue means the two endpoints touch.
Reject an endpoint pair if its middle cells cannot add to the clue. Remove a candidate only if every possible arrangement rules it out.

copy.description: Row 1 has a sandwich clue of 20 and a 1 in R1C8. Try possible places for 9 and add only the digits between it and R1C8.

guide.start: Find the possible places for 1 and 9. Either can be closer to the clue. Leave both out of the sum.
guide.check: For each pair of endpoints, add the digits strictly between them. A zero clue means the two endpoints touch.
guide.reason: Reject an endpoint pair if its middle cells cannot add to the clue. Remove a candidate only if every possible arrangement rules it out.

lessons.title: X-sums
lessons.summary: An X-sum adds cells from the clue end of a row or column. The first digit tells you how many cells to include and counts toward the sum itself. A first digit of 3 means the first three cells add to the clue.

blocks.title: Try a length from the first cell

paragraphs: Start at the cell nearest the clue. Its digit is both the number of cells to count and the first digit in the sum. For example, if the first digit is 3, add the first three cells. Try each candidate in the first cell as a possible length.
If no sum of that length matches the clue, remove that first digit. For later cells, keep candidates that fit at least one possible arrangement.

copy.description: The clue is 32. If R1C1 were 9, the sum would include the whole row and equal 45. Remove 9 from R1C1.

guide.start: Start at the cell nearest the clue. Its digit is both the number of cells to count and the first digit in the sum.
guide.check: For example, if the first digit is 3, add the first three cells. Try each candidate in the first cell as a possible length.
guide.reason: If no sum of that length matches the clue, remove that first digit. For later cells, keep candidates that fit at least one possible arrangement.

groups.title: Quadruple Sudoku
groups.overview: Use the printed digits in a circle to narrow its four surrounding cells.

lessons.title: Quadruple
lessons.summary: A Quadruple circle tells you which digits must appear in the four cells that touch it. Each printed digit needs its own cell. If the circle lists all four digits, it accounts for every cell around it.

blocks.title: Match the printed digits to the four cells

paragraphs: Four printed digits fill the four cells around a circle. Cross out any other candidate in those cells.
With fewer printed digits, some cells can contain other digits. Match each printed digit to a separate surrounding cell before removing a candidate.

copy.description: The circle between R6C3, R6C4, R7C3, and R7C4 lists 2, 4, 6, and 8. These four cells need those four digits.
copy.reason: The four printed digits fill all four cells. There is no cell left for 5, so remove candidate 5 from R6C3.

paragraphs: Count repeated printed digits separately. A circle with 2, 2, and 6 needs two different cells containing 2 and another containing 6.
The usual house rules still apply. Cells sharing a row, column, or region cannot contain the same digit.

blocks.title: Use a circle inside a box

paragraphs: In Clover’s linked puzzle, the circle at R2C1, R2C2, R3C1, and R3C2 lists 5, 7, and 9. All four cells belong to box 1.
The circle requires 5, 7, and 9 inside box 1. Remove those digits from the other cells in box 1.

guide.start: Read every printed digit in the circle. Count repeated digits separately.
guide.check: Fit each printed digit to a separate surrounding cell. Apply the row, column, and region rules.
guide.reason: Remove a candidate only when no complete assignment for the four cells can use it.

references.label: Sudoku Coach constructor and rule description

groups.title: Algebraic Cages
groups.overview: Find the possible cage totals when several cages use the same letter.

lessons.title: Algebraic cage bounds
lessons.summary: A letter in a cage label is a shared positive integer. Compare the smallest and largest totals for cages with the same letter. Their ranges can narrow the letter to one value or rule out candidates in a cage.

blocks.title: Find cages that share a letter

paragraphs: Look for the same letter on two or more cages. Start with a short cage or one with filled cells. Add the smallest and largest distinct digits the cage can use. Each sum gives an endpoint for its possible total.

Convert each cage’s total range into a range for the letter. If the label is n+2, subtract 2 from both endpoints. Keep only the values all cages allow. Use that common range to check which candidates can still fit each cage.
In the example, n is 5 even though the grid uses digits 1 to 4. The letter gives you a cage total. Only a digit can fill a cell.

blocks.title: Try it on another grid
Check your move

questions.prompt: Which candidate can you remove from R2C1?
questions.explanation: The m+2 cage has at most 3+4, so m is at most 5. Then m−2 is at most 3. Remove candidate 4 from R2C1.

questions.prompt: If m is 5, which digits can fill the m+2 cage?
questions.explanation: The cage total is 7. The only distinct digits from 1 to 4 that add to 7 are 3 and 4. These clues allow either order.
